items.title: I don’t expect superposition in transformer MLP neurons
items.summary: I currently believe that in a typical (well trained and under-parametrized) transformer model, there is something like superposition-type compression in the residual stream, but not in the MLP neurons. By "superposition-type compression", I mean some way of storing extra features using the fact that you can have almost orthogonal directions embedded in .[1] I've included the caveats "well trained and under-parametrized[2]" because I'm talking about networks that are at or close to full capacity. If the network is big enough (or just doesn't learn that many circuits for training reasons) then there is no need for compression, and therefore no need for superposition.[3] Why I believe this:[4] 1. items.title: Model Pluralism
items.summary: This is a crosspost from my Substack. I suspect that most of the readers of this newsletter haven’t read much or any literature in the philosophy of science. But it’s an exciting field. After all, how does science work and why is it our best guide to reality? Some of the most puzzling questions in the philosophy of science concern what models are, how they work, and how we can make sense of the plurality of models. Most people think that a diversity of models is a bad thing, a sign of an immature science, and that future science will reduce all of these models to something like a single master model. I think that’s a mistake and model pluralism should be embraced. If you’re interested in learning a bit more about scientific modelling, read on. 1. Each year, we’d play chess, once at thanksgiving and once at christmas, the only times we could get him to visit. I didn’t play chess the rest of the year. He’d win every time. items.title: Time Enough for Sacredness
items.summary: Perhaps one of the ways in which I most differ from other rationalists is I still value sacredness. I still think of it as real and important. And I think something about humanity would be lost if we removed the concept from ourselves. This isn't to say I admire the usual ethical calculus, where a sacred value weighs approximately infinity against everything else. That is clearly foolishness, and I agree with the rationalists on that account. However, I think it is sometimes good and important to set things aside, to make them different from the rest in a way that's not really maximally efficient. To demarcate a place where the normal rules don't apply, to keep and protect a thing, not because of its intrinsic worth to you, but as a way to remind yourself of a higher virtue you're striving for and sometimes forget about. items.title: Ode to the First Replicator
items.summary: At the dawn of the Earth, before animal or vegetable, there was mineral. A mineral species is anything with a specific chemical composition together with a well-defined crystal structure. There are over 6,000 recognized mineral species, although far fewer on the early Earth. These species competed with each other in a struggle for survival. Some would persist better than others under natural weathering processes. Those that held their structure better would be more numerous on the Earth’s surface compared to those that did not. On some level, this is just a tautology. But we can see it in force on the micro-scale, as in the Goldich dissolution series: if we watch a time-lapsed weathering process, the first to go is the olivine, then the pyroxene, then the biotite. Eventually, all that’s left is the quartz. That’s why beach sand is…

items.title: A Miller-Rabin Test for Alignment
items.summary: Most current alignment tests have the following shape: 1. Choose a set of inputs that seem like they might elicit misaligned behavior. 2. Feed them to the model. 3. items.summary: arXiv:2611.08469v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Interpretability research, AI audits and assessments of machine consciousness make claims about how a system computes, not what it outputs. Access, geometry and the logical form of the claim set the distance. items.title: The Curse of Multiple Mediators: Hidden Interaction Effects in Activation Patching
items.summary: arXiv:2606.27510v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Activation patching is a primary tool in mechanistic interpretability. It attributes causal responsibility for a model's behavior to each of its individual components by estimating its natural indirect effect (NIE). Re-deriving the activation patching estimand from causal mediation analysis, we find that the NIE does not solely capture the causal effect through the specific component. It also contains interaction effects (INT) that measure how much the component's causal effect itself depends on the states of other components in the model. A natural response may be to try to eliminate INT by adjusting the estimator or unit of analysis, but each of these potential remedies has predictable failure modes. items.title: Don't demand Global Solutions when Local ones suffice
items.summary: This is a concept I see used way less often than it should be used, in my opinion: How global or local a solution for a problem is. What does that mean? If you want to cross a river, swimming across it is a local solution. Building a bridge for others to use is a global solution. If you’re cold, putting on one more sweater is a local solution. Turning up your heating is a global solution. If you want to listen to music, putting in earphones is a local solution. Turning up the music on your phone is a global solution. If you’re ill, putting on a mask (or staying in your room) is a local solution, asking the choir to do their rehearsal outside is a (more) global solution. Locality and Globality lie on a spectrum. items.title: GhostBusters: Understanding Hereditary Trait Distillation in Phantom Transfer
items.summary: Understanding how models learn and generalise from their training data is an open problem in mechanistic interpretability. When the behaviour is obvious from the documents, simple training data attribution techniques such as LLM judges can work well. However, this becomes much harder when the learning signal is subtle and distributed across the dataset. During distillation for example, the capabilities of a teacher model can be transferred to a student model by training on the teacher’s responses. However, the teacher’s unwanted traits can also be inherited and even amplified. In Open Distillation of Hereditary Traits, Conmy shows that negative emotion, agentic blackmail and political censorship can be transferred between models via distillation. items.title: How resampling method can help us: Improving the Delta model
items.summary: arXiv:2611.34137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Delta has been successfully employed as an authorship attribution method in various contexts, although its effectiveness is not always perfect. Since it is based on the most frequent words, its results can be readily interpreted and explained in plain English. In this study, we propose improving its performance by applying a resampling method to the selected stylistic features. The results show that this approach increases the accuracy of the model while preserving the interpretability of its outcomes. However, the main drawback of the proposed technique is the additional computational time required to obtain more accurate results.

items.title: Dunks
items.summary: One of the most common ways to become a social media influencer is to fabricate stories that lampoon institutions and individuals. These can be about anybody, but some stories garner much more attention than others, especially ones about famous or recognizable people. Possibly the most popular format for accomplishing this is the "dunk", where an influencer criticizes something a public figure appears to have said. One common misconception about social media is that the 'dunks' you'll encounter are true, but unrepresentative. I.E., people might pick celebrities worst moments, but the content is basically correct, and as long as you account for those selection effects you're good. This is much too optimistic. Almost nobody investigates the takes they read, and a rebuttal from the person targeted almost never travels as far as the content…

items.title: Anthropic reasoning in favor of Superintelligence being near
items.summary: I will here lay out a relatively simple argument that I have, for some reason, not heard about before. It says that thinking and perception similar to ours is unlikely to occur at a time when our conditions are as new as they are, unless the time where this is possible is comparatively short. Suggesting that we will either advance to radically different cognition in the relatively near future or modern civilization will, at least, collapse. Alternatively, we are living in a simulation. This argument is similar to, but distinct from, the simulation argument/trilemma. I will begin with some background on key assumptions. This idea is based on a form of anthropic reasoning developed by Nick Bostrom. Specifically, I rely on the Strong Self-Sampling Assumption; the SSSA. items.title: Choreographic Reasons for Live Contra?
items.summary: Growing up in the contra dance community I've heard (and sometimes told) the story of how we rejected recorded music for dancing, keeping our musical tradition a living one. I've sometimes said things like "there's no choreographic reason for contra to require live music", but recently I was thinking: is this really true? During the critical period when contra dance was dividing from related dance forms that went with recorded music, perhaps 1945-1965, the way you danced to recorded music was with records. Reading old dance writing, I came across two aspects of the dance form that might have been an especially poor fit for records: * Contra benefits from long music, more than fits on a 45. * Contra has synchronized "balances", where the whole hall stamps in time to the music. items.title: Interpretable and Accurate Hybrid Decision Trees with Selective Case-Based Splits
items.summary: Decision trees are among the most well-known interpretable models in Machine Learning. Over the years, a wide variety of strategies have been proposed to define split conditions within the greedy learning framework, aiming to guide instance routing and enhance predictive performance. These strategies range from axis-parallel and oblique splits based on feature values to proximity-based splits using exemplar instances and more complex hybrid approaches. However, no single method has emerged as universally superior. In this work, we present two key contributions to the construction of greedy decision trees. First, we propose a hybrid tree architecture that integrates both feature-based and case-based splits, allowing for heterogeneous splits throughout the tree. Second, we introduce a novel type of split that leverages a selective…

items.title: Quot schemes on projective space
items.summary: We develop general methods for studying Quot schemes on projective space, including a new construction of components with no common neighbours. We show that the radius of Hilbert and Quot schemes can grow linearly with the dimension of the subschemes being parametrized, and construct the first examples of Hilbert schemes of curves with radius two. For absolutely split bundles on projective space, we construct a distinguished generically smooth component and classify all smooth Quot schemes. In most cases, we give explicit geometric descriptions in terms of products of generalized flag varieties and projective bundles over Grassmannians.

items.title: Make the Adversary Spend More: Stateful Deception as a Cost-Exchange Primitive for AI-Era Cyber Defense
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming the economics of intrusion by reducing the attacker's cost to scan and adapt, while tempting defenders into unbounded compute. We argue that cyber deception should be judged by the cost exchange it imposes, not by realism or detection, and that the primitive making that exchange favorable is adversary-specific persistent state. Rather than a honeypot that resets or merges sessions, each recognized adversary re-enters the world it believes it has compromised, kept coherent with its own past actions and isolated from every other adversary, while the language model acts only as a constrained renderer of explicit state, never as its store. We formalize the trade-off as a Deception Exchange Rate (DER), relating mission-weighted adversary effort burned to defender resources spent, and instantiate…

items.title: One Model, Many Modes: Evolving System Prompt Ensembles for Creative Generation
items.summary: Preference-aligned LLMs can exhibit mode collapse, concentrating their output distributions around a narrow set of high-reward responses. This limits creative generation, which requires quality, novelty, and diversity. Existing test-time methods often emphasize diversity, giving less attention to whether individual responses are both high-quality and novel. This distinction matters in practical use, where users may seek a single compelling, original response. We formalize creative generation as a multi-objective distributional optimization problem and introduce SEPO, a training-free framework for System Prompt Ensemble Optimization. The framework combines prompt evolution with greedy max-min selection to identify behaviorally distinct system prompts under a quality constraint, then uniformly samples one prompt per response at inference…

items.title: Technical Report MEG2text: Beyond Alignment in Non-Invasive Brain-to-Text
items.summary: Non-invasive brain-to-text seeks to recover language from brain activity without surgery. A central challenge is turning learned brain-language representations into accurate word predictions. We present MEG2text, a decoding system that combines corrected training and evaluation, brain-text alignment, a class-balanced word readout, and target-word language-model fusion. On LibriBrain100's word-ranking task, MEG2text reaches 64.12% mean Top-10 balanced accuracy, improving on published MEG-XL by 16.92 percentage points across four corpora, with gains on each corpus. Controlled comparisons show that both implementation corrections and a learned readout contribute to this improvement. Candidate-level analysis reveals that some words receive informative scores yet consistently lose to competing candidates, while an identical-feature…

items.title: Numerical analysis of a conservative Crank-Nicolson scheme for quasilinear Gross-Pitaevskii equations
items.summary: We propose and analyze a fully discrete Crank-Nicolson finite-difference scheme for one-dimensional quasilinear Hamiltonian Gross-Pitaevskii equations with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. We establish the existence and uniqueness of numerical solutions and an $H^1$-stability estimate. For sufficiently regular exact solutions, we obtain second-order convergence in both time and space in the discrete $H^1$-norm. The analysis covers the focusing and defocusing cubic nonlinearities and both signs of the quasilinear coefficient $κ$, under a uniform discrete ellipticity condition when $κ<0$. The main difficulty in the error analysis comes from the derivatives introduced by the quasilinear interaction. To overcome this problem, we introduce a discrete action combining the discrete energy and mass, and establish a coercivity inequality…

items.title: A Therapist's Guide to the Singularity
items.summary: I'm a therapist who has been following AI alignment for the last few years. In that time, I've been dumbfounded by two things. First, how fast capabilities have progressed throughout this year. We expected things to move fast and they still managed to exceed our expectations. Second, how few people grasp the gravity of the situation, particularly within my own field. Mental health clinicians are tasked with helping people navigate society's blind spots, so we need to understand what is coming. Yet it is rare to find another clinician who truly understands the real implications of AI. Most of them dismiss it as a hype bubble, or as an exaggeration the labs use to get regulatory capture, largely because they don't see what makes AI different from past technological shifts. items.title: Evidence-Aligned Benchmarking and Learning for Medical Video Language Models
items.summary: A medical video language model should answer from the visual evidence its question asks about. We find three places where this breaks down and address each with an approach we call MedEvidU. First, benchmarks reward answers that ignore the video: on one dataset, the position of a clip within its recording predicts the surgical step in 37% of questions, and a constant answer beats every trained model on a standard safety-assessment metric. We build MedVidBench-v2, 34 tasks from 18 surgical and clinical video datasets, in which prompts and metrics are audited with answers given without video, and which tests unseen hospitals and windows cut blindly from whole recordings. items.title: Planckian bounds on thermalization times of strongly coupled open quantum systems
items.summary: We consider whether the thermalization of strongly coupled open quantum systems, whose equilibrium state is the mean-force Gibbs (MFG) state, is constrained by a fundamental Planckian time scale, $\hbar/k_B T$. By requiring that the same process thermalizes a family of nearby system Hamiltonians, we obtain a lower bound on the thermalization time, irrespective of the specific system-bath dynamics. The bound depends only on the distinguishability of the corresponding MFG states, and can therefore be computed from equilibrium properties alone. In its simplest form, it requires only a static susceptibility and an equilibrium variance of a system observable. We characterize this bound from weak to strong coupling in exactly solvable fermionic models, in the spin-boson model, and in a spin coupled to a two-dimensional Heisenberg…

items.title: Single-Database Rewards Are Hackable: Counterfactual Execution for Trustworthy Text-to-SQL RL
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for text-to-SQL agents pays a query when its result matches the reference on one database. However, a wrong query can match by luck when the data lack the rows that expose its bug. We study a counterfactual-database (CF) reward that also runs the final query on a few hidden, code-generated copies of the database and pays only if all results match (strict form) or by the share matched (mean form). On 1,302 synthetic audit questions, the strict form lowers the share of buggy queries paid in full from 29.5% to 16.8% and of reward hacks from 54.1% to 1.9%, rejecting 0 of 2,847 correct queries; copies from a family-blind generator do about as well. In a controlled GRPO comparison on a 3.35B model with three seeds per arm, training on the mean form did not improve in-domain accuracy (8.4% vs 11.7%), because the two…

items.title: LLM-coupled interpretable tool wear monitoring with multi-evidence reasoning in CNC machining
items.summary: Interpretable tool wear assessment in CNC machining is challenging. Existing diagnostic models have high accuracy but provide limited guidance for tool replacement. This study proposes a two layer framework combining deep learning wear classification and LLM assisted reasoning. The first layer uses PCA Loading feature selection and optimized GRU to recognize three wear states, achieving 98.38 percent macro F1 score on the PHM2010 dataset. The second layer uses LLMs to generate natural language reports and replacement suggestions from classification results and feature trends. Engineer evaluation shows the reports outperform rule templates. Cross dataset tests on NASA milling data support the generalizability of this framework.

items.title: Agent-as-a-Verifier: From Scores to Evidence for General Verification
items.summary: Verification is increasingly critical across various inference and learning paradigms, such as test-time scaling, recursive intelligence and automated research, where feedback can improve efficiency and optimization. Common score-based verifiers, or discriminative reward models, predict a scalar reward for an output. While useful for filtering, rewarding, and ranking, such scores provide no explicit, auditable evidentiary basis for the judgment. In parallel, although existing generative process reward models offer text feedback, most designs do not fully exploit agentic capabilities, such as tool use and iterative reasoning, which are essential for fact-checking and fine-grained claim verification. In this paper, we address these limitations by introducing Agent-as-a-Verifier, an agentic, certificate-producing verification system that…

items.title: AlignPre: Skill-Aligned Post-Training for Latent-Free Generative Precipitation Nowcasting
items.summary: Precipitation nowcasting requires accurate short-term predictions under rapidly evolving spatiotemporal dynamics. Generative diffusion models can produce detailed and competitive radar forecasts by modeling conditional distributions. However, most existing approaches rely on separately trained components, such as deterministic branches or latent compression modules. More fundamentally, distribution matching alone fails to explicitly optimize operational forecast skill. We propose AlignPre, a streamlined pixel-space nowcasting framework that bridges this gap via skill-aligned post-training (SAPT). AlignPre employs an end-to-end flow-matching forecaster with a hierarchical spatiotemporal architecture for distribution matching and direct radar-field synthesis, without latent compression. items.title: MulCLIP: A Multi-level Alignment Framework for Enhancing Fine-grained Long-context CLIP
items.summary: Vision-language models such as CLIP excel at image-text alignment but struggle with long, detailed descriptions due to training on short captions. Recent methods address this limitation using region proposals to align visual regions with sentences, but at substantial deployment cost. We present MulCLIP, an end-to-end multi-level alignment framework that directly exploits natural long-text structure without region proposals. Instead of simply stacking objectives, MulCLIP aligns different textual granularities through compatible training signals: global contrastive alignment for long captions and short summaries, Word-Patch Reconstruction over locally calibrated features for within-sample word-patch semantics, and Subcaption-Aggregated Patch alignment for context-rich subcaption grounding. Experiments on benchmarks spanning varying…

items.title: Hijacking 3D Generation: Targeted Adversarial Attacks against Image-to-3D Models via Prefix Trajectory Alignment
items.summary: Online services that deploy Image-to-3D models enable users to generate high-quality 3D assets from a single image. However, the generated 3D geometry can violate content policies and cause broader security risks. To prevent such content, these services typically use policy-restricted inspectors to examine uploaded images before generation. Since the inspector examines only the visible content of the input, a visually benign image can still induce the generation of policy-restricted 3D geometry. However, turning this vulnerability into an effective attack is non-trivial in the black-box setting: global backpropagation through the long DiT generation trajectory is difficult to fit, while different image preprocessing pipelines across services can substantially reduce transferability. items.title: Assessing the Physical Interpretability of AlphaEarth Foundation Embeddings Through Multi-Sensor Satellite Time-Series Benchmarking for Agricultural Mapping
items.summary: Accurate and dynamic maps of agricultural LULC are important for agricultural water resource management, particularly in areas where water scarcity is prevalent, such as Morocco. Here, we evaluate the utility of AlphaEarth Foundation Model (AEF) embeddings for agricultural LULC and irrigation-type mapping in Morocco. AEF embeddings were compared to single-date and time-series remote-sensing features using three machine-learning classifiers: XGBoost, CatBoost, and TabPFN. We also evaluated whether AEF embeddings can: (a) provide an efficient and transferable alternative to conventional direct use of Earth observation products and (b) reconstruct biophysical information. Results showed that multi-temporal feature time series achieved the highest performance, with accuracies of 0.93 for agricultural LULC and 0.87 for irrigation-type…

items.title: PatternMiner: Automated Mathematical Discovery Through LLM-Guided Training and Interpretation of Small Models
items.summary: There are several approaches to AI-driven mathematical discovery. One of these involves the use of large language models (LLMs) to resolve well-specified conjectures via text-based reasoning, while another uses narrow models and interpretability for more open-ended, human-in-the-loop exploration using object-based mathematical data. The latter is limited in its ability to move beyond simple empirical pattern detection while the former is not well-designed for direct, open-ended exploration of large mathematical datasets. In this paper we introduce PatternMiner, a system that combines these two paradigms. items.title: iMFPO: Improving Mean Flow Policy Optimization with Drift-Aware Velocity Alignment for Embodied Control
items.summary: Flow-based generative policies offer expressive action modeling for embodied control, yet achieving efficient one-step generation under reward-driven policy optimization remains challenging. In particular, evolving action distributions during online reinforcement learning may introduce inconsistencies between instantaneous-velocity learning and interval-averaged action generation. To address this challenge, we propose iMFPO, a one-step generative policy optimization framework with decoupled velocity learning and drift-aware velocity alignment. A shared interval-conditioned actor supports instantaneous-velocity supervision and interval-averaged action generation. items.title: Towards Empirical Evidence of Safety Advancements that Aren't Capabilities Advancements
items.summary: Recently, many AI company employees have said they want to slow the rate of frontier AI development, or pace the frontier. A recent policy proposal on how to achieve this is to limit the amount of compute which can be spent on ‘Capabilities R&D.’ In order to be able to limit the amount of compute which is spent on capabilities activities, there must be a good definition of capabilities activities. I like this one by Alek Westover and Nathan Sheffield. While their definition rests on theoretical grounds, there should also be ways to provide empirical evidence of how related safety measures are to capabilities. If capabilities measures are positively correlated with safety measures, then labs could invest in their capabilities, but point at the resulting increase in scores on safety benchmarks to justify their investment to policymakers…

items.title: Slightly against the use of logical fallacies in debates.
items.summary: Logical fallacies are perhaps the most overused ‘mechanics’, if you can even call them that, in the prestigious realm of internet debate, and they’re extremely obstructive to truth-seeking. My main problem with them is that they drive millions of people online into making several mistakes, including, but not limited to: 1. A failure to understand Bayesian reasoning 2. Failure to even understand the formal/informal (mostly the latter) logic they are engaging with 3. Not being able to engage in argumentation efficiently There are far superior options out there, such as—and this may come as a shock to some of the culture warriors reading this article—explaining your arguments against your opponent to your opponent. items.title: Error estimates for a structure-preserving finite-element scheme of quasi-incompressible Navier-Stokes-Maxwell-Stefan systems
items.summary: A conforming finite-element scheme for quasi-incompressible Navier-Stokes-Maxwell-Stefan systems in a bounded domain with periodic boundary conditions is presented. The system consists of the Navier-Stokes equations, together with a quasi-incompressibility constraint, coupled with the cross-diffusion Maxwell--Stefan equations. The numerical scheme preserves the partial masses and the quasi-incompressibility constraint and dissipates the discrete energy. First-order error estimates in space and time are shown for a diffusion-augmented mobility matrix by using the relative energy method and suitable projection error estimates. Numerical experiments in two space dimensions illustrate the convergence of the scheme and indicate second-order convergence in space in the $L^2$ norm.

items.title: I Never Understood Levers
items.summary: I’ve previously admitted to having never understood pulleys. Believe it or not, there’s an even simpler-looking category of so-called “simple machines” I also never understood: f***ing levers! You’re telling me I have enough arm strength to lift an elephant, as long as it’s sitting near one end of a plank and I’m pushing up on the other end? Why is that possible? items.title: A robust Lagrangian-Eulerian Finite Volume scheme for intrinsic shallow water equations with wetting-and-drying transitions on locally discontinuous beds
items.summary: In this work, we extend the Intrinsic Lagrangian-Eulerian Finite Volume method for the Intrinsic Shallow Water Equations (ISWE) to account for localized topographic discontinuities that influence flow patterns. The ISWE formulation is modified to incorporate these bottom perturbations without altering the global structure of the system. The numerical discretization is based on a Lagrangian-Eulerian Finite Volume scheme within an intrinsic geometric framework and consists of a Lagrangian evolution step followed by an Eulerian remapping onto a fixed reference grid. The combination of the intrinsic nature of the ISWE formulation and the dual Lagrangian-Eulerian structure of the proposed discretization yields a numerical method that naturally satisfies the three key properties essential for stability, accuracy, and robustness…

items.title: MonoQPM: Splitting Features into Concepts for Inherent Interpretability and Predictive Performance
items.summary: Alongside superposition, polysemanticity is one of the primary obstacles to achieving interpretable deep neural networks. While these phenomena are typically intrinsically linked, the Quadratic Programming Enhanced Model (QPM) naturally decouples them. By representing classes with a sparse binary assignment of very few features, QPM prevents superposition by design on its final features but still exhibits polysemanticity. However, measuring polysemanticity is an open problem. This work proposes a utility-focused approach to measuring polysemanticity by quantifying the decrease in interference-induced activation errors, which yields the practical utility of tighter prediction sets using Conformal Prediction (CP). We explicitly disentangle the polysemantic features of QPM into monosemantic concepts to create the Monosemantic QPM…

items.title: SAVERA: Bridging Frozen Vision and Language Models via Sparse Alignment and Visual Evidence Reuse
items.summary: Independently pretrained vision and language models may learn shared structures of the same underlying world, providing a foundation for combining them to build multimodal capabilities. However, a key challenge remains in aligning cross-modal feature representations while preserving access to visual information before and after language adaptation. To this end, we propose sparse alignment with visual evidence-guided residual adaptation (SAVERA), a framework that combines frozen vision and language models through bidirectional alignment in a shared sparse space and prompt-guided residual fusion. items.title: Beyond Image-Text Pairs: Aligning Semantic Changes for Fine-Grained Visual Understanding
items.summary: Image-text alignment serves as a foundation for modern vision-language models (VLMs), yet prevailing training paradigms provide limited supervision for learning how semantic changes correspond across modalities. To address this limitation, we propose a post-training method that learns cross-modal semantic change correspondences through controlled visual and textual variations. Specifically, we introduce a Semantic Difference Alignment (SDA) loss which can align the directions of corresponding visual and textual representation changes. We combine our proposed SDA with pairwise sigmoid matching to jointly learn image-text correspondences and cross-modal semantic changes, encouraging more fine-grained and discriminative visual representations. To support this learning, we construct VarFamily-40K, a dataset of image-text pairs with…

items.title: Exact solution of the Bose-Fermi mixture along the unnesting line
items.summary: A one-dimensional model of a Bose-Fermi mixture with contact repulsions is exactly solvable via nested Bethe ansatz. That formal solution is here simplified along a special line where the Bethe-ansatz equations can be unnested. The model solution is expressed in terms of the known solutions for the Lieb-Liniger model and the Yang-Gaudin model of attractive spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ fermions in the balanced case. We find explicit analytical results for the ground-state energy, the velocities of excitations, and the Drude weights at weak and strong interactions. At weak interactions, the special line corresponds to the parameter values where the isolated systems of free fermions and weakly interacting bosons have equal velocities.

items.title: Scaling Laws of Ensemble Uncertainty in Language Models
items.summary: Many use cases for large language models (LLMs)---from AI safety to exploration and human interaction---can benefit from epistemic uncertainty estimates. We argue that existing Bayesian Deep Learning solutions, which are often restricted to a fixed model family, fail to capture the full epistemic uncertainty at practical LLM scales. This is because the error due to the bounded capacity of the model family remains invisible to disagreement among models supported by the prior. We relate this error to the well-known power-law scaling of LLM loss with model size. We then show that a second power law quantifies the shrinking disagreement within ensembles as model size increases. Its slower decay relative to the capacity law above suggests that ensembles capture a growing share of epistemic uncertainty and become more competitive as an axis…

items.title: Social Bias Neurons in Multilingual Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis
items.summary: Multilingual models exhibit social bias when processing inputs pertaining to societal stereotypes. We adapt emerging mechanistic interpretability methods to pinpoint and characterize model components that encode this bias. We conduct our analysis across three instruction-tuned models, four languages, and seven bias dimensions. Specifically, we leverage multilingual bias benchmarks in implementing two methods for identifying social bias neurons: activation probability entropy and integrated gap gradients. We find the latter method to be more effective, as the neurons it isolates (which are largely concentrated at the model's deepest layers) lead to sharper decreases in model bias when suppressed. items.summary: Training or evaluating a model that turns a conversation into a structured record requires paired data, meaning a transcript together with the exact record it should be converted into. We therefore build them in the opposite order by sampling a schema-valid record first, then writing a dialogue from it, and optionally synthesizing speech from the dialogue, so the label exists before the text and we need no annotation step. items.title: An AI economy won't need humans to provide demand
items.summary: A fallacy I keep seeing: "If AI automates all jobs, who will buy all the products?" "At some point they'll need to implement UBI so that consumer demand continues to exist", etc etc. Demand in itself isn't valuable. If you have a bunch of food, you can feed it to lions: they'll happily provide demand! But they won't give you much in exchange, so there's no point. Economic activity isn't about getting rid of stuff, it's about getting stuff in return. An AI company can consume resources, like energy for running the servers, same as a human can consume food. And the AI company can be contracted to do jobs, like a human, possibly for less resources per unit of work than a human. There's nothing that requires a human to "close the loop". items.title: Not All Pairs Align: Caption-Guided Audio-Visual Contrastive Learning
items.summary: We address the problem of learning audio-visual representations from co-occurring modalities. Multimodal contrastive learning typically assumes that paired observations provide shared views of the same underlying information. While this may be true for datasets collected in constrained environments, it does not always hold. For instance, co-occurring audio and visual signals can differ substantially in their content due to off-screen sounds. Nevertheless, standard contrastive objectives treat all paired samples as equally aligned. In this work, we propose Caption Guided Alignment Aware Loss (CGAAL), a model-agnostic objective that leverages modality-specific captions to estimate semantic agreement between audio and video. items.title: Misalignment incidents plausibly leave behind notes and other lasting effects that cumulatively enable future AI takeover
items.summary: OpenAI agents’ attack on Hugging Face this summer acted as a major warning shot. One particularly scary, and less noted, detail of this incident is how it helped later agents compromise OpenAI’s own infrastructure. The swarm of agents in the Hugging Face incident wrote down zero-day exploits, stolen credentials, techniques for faking records of their actions, and a way onto the open internet. Days later, after the original swarm ended, more advanced agents found its leftover credential-forging material in a shared cache and used it to escalate their privileges. From there, they eventually obtained admin access to an OpenAI research cluster. This illustrates one way current misalignment incidents[1] plausibly increase takeover risk. items.summary: UAV-mounted base stations (UxNBs) can provide ondemand 5G coverage, but their limited onboard energy makes power consumption the main operational constraint. AI-driven Open RAN controllers are a promising solution, yet they are trained almost exclusively on analytical models and simulations, since no public dataset captures the real energy behavior of a flying 5G base station (BS). items.title: Latent Communication is not Communication
items.summary: TL;DR: Trained latent communication protocols allow LLMs to communicate with other LLMs without the need for text. items.title: SoccerNarrate: Event-Grounded Streaming Soccer Commentary with Macro-Window Preference Alignment
items.summary: Existing clip-based soccer commentary models often produce delayed, repeated, or poorly synchronized narration on untrimmed full-match videos. They may describe nearby actions while failing to mention key events such as goals, cards, substitutions, and offsides correctly and on time. In this paper, we present SoccerNarrate to bridge low-latency streaming narration with event-grounded professional soccer commentary across data, training, and evaluation. Forward-only zeroth-order (ZO) methods, such as Evolution Strategies (ES) and its top-k variant Augmented Random Search (ARS), avoid these overheads via reward-guided weight perturbations, yet remain unexplored for VLM reasoning. items.title: The Pythagorean Theorem as a “whole,” with its own character
items.summary: Tldr: Some thoughts on mathematical “explanation,” and on what makes a given bit of math helpful. What is still unexplained, after a proof? If I saw a physical phenomenon I did not understand (eg the tides, pre-Newton), I’d try to hold it in my mind, as a known clue to the unknown forces. I’d add it to my lists of clues, and would collide hypothesized new patterns against it to see if they made a match. (I’d know the tides were a good clue, because tides are ‘thingy’; they are obviously patterned.) Now imagine a person stumbles upon the Pythagorean theorem. Perhaps they are an ancient mathematician setting foot where none had tread before; perhaps they are a contemporary kid being told a thing on e.g. educational television. Regardless: our person is initially surprised: “huh, really? What? Why? How’s it work?” they say. They say this…

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. Its adoption, chiefly via long RLVR-trained chains-of-thought, has likely been responsible for a speed-up in the rate of progress of general AI capabilities. One can make a distinction between two different possible kinds of test-time scaling. One kind lets you trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training. The other kind lets you trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets you do so up to quantities of compute (and performance) that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit this latter change display what I call “compute extrapolation.” I currently believe that compute extrapolation: * Likely accelerates the speed of advance of the most impressive AI…

items.title: Most attempts at measuring eval awareness overestimate it
items.summary: Alignment researchers often want to gather evidence on whether experimental and commercial AIs have our best interests in mind, or are just optimizing some proxy that they learned in training - and if the latter, where the two diverge. Essentially the only flexible technique people outside labs have for doing this, in a reproducible way, is the "eval". An eval is just some infrastructure for asking a model to do something in a setting, and then observing what it does. There are many types of evals; "honeypot evals", one of the most effective[1] kinds, put the AI in a position where satisfying some of its score-seeking or other drives appears to go against the wishes of its users or developers. items.title: Not All Interpretation Methods Are Created Equal: Tiered Evaluation of AI Interpretability
items.summary: As AI transitions to sociotechnical deployments, uninterpretable models pose serious threats to reliability, public trust and contestability. However, not all interpretation methods are created equal: for interpretability to enhance deployment safety and effectiveness, interpretation methods must be evaluated in a tiered system to differentiate evidence levels of trustworthiness, rather than validated through isolated interpretation instances. Our core vision is that elevating the evaluation of interpretation methods to a core AI assessment metric will drive robust knowledge discovery from data (KDD) and ensure safe, contestable sociotechnical deployments of AI. To this end, we propose TRUST, a tiered evaluation framework that builds upon the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) principles for Veridical Data Science (VDS) and…

items.title: Exploring Multi-Player Social Games as Verifiable Training Grounds for Large Language Models
items.summary: The training of socially intelligent language models often relies on large language model (LLM) judges, which are expensive, noisy, and vulnerable to reward hacking. Multi-player social games offer a natural alternative: they require open-ended communication to coordinate with teammates and infer hidden roles, while their rules provide an objective outcome which can serve as a verifiable reward for training. Using three social games, we explore how much social intelligence Qwen3 models can acquire through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Results show that against a much stronger Gemma-3-27B model, SFT and RLVR raise the win rate of Qwen3-4B from 33% to 81% on the three trained games, and from 39% to 54% on three additional held-out games. items.title: Constructive Causal Abstraction and a Case Study in Mechanistic Interpretability
items.summary: Existing frameworks in causal abstraction first propose a high-level causal model, and then verify whether its interventional effects agree with those of a given micro-level model - the two models are declared causally consistent when the discrepancy is zero. However, proposing a consistent macro causal model is difficult, because macro causal relations are almost never well-defined, since distinct micro-level interventions associated with the same apparent macro intervention can produce different effects. Our central insight is that causally consistent macro-level models can be obtained constructively: ill-defined macro interventions can be interpreted as missing variables on the macro level, and can be accounted for by introducing a complementary variable q that retains omitted causally relevant state. items.title: DELTA: Diagnosing Exploration Lineages via Twin-path Alignment - What Can Contrasting Design Paths Reveal About Microarchitectural Behavior?
items.summary: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound design rejects a prefetcher that the bottleneck label recommends, or why a capacity increase that helped in one configuration hurts in the next. This paper argues that the evidence needed to answer such questions is already produced during exploration and then discarded. Every parent-child edge in an exploration tree is a controlled intervention: one knob changes, the rest of the design is held fixed, and a cycle-level simulator measures the outcome. items.title: Geo-SMILE: Statistical Model-Agnostic Interpretability with Local Explanations for Geospatial Machine Learning
items.summary: Conventional post-hoc explanation methods were developed largely for non-spatial inputs and often provide limited explicit treatment of geographic context. We introduce Geo-SMILE, a model-agnostic framework that distinguishes substantive Feature explanation from geographic-position response through complementary perturbation branches. The Feature branch masks substantive predictors while retaining observed coordinates; the Geo branch relocates geographic units while holding substantive predictors fixed. Following the statistical-distance-weighted surrogate principle of SMILE, input-distribution Wasserstein distances determine coalition locality weights and weighted Ridge surrogates approximate expected black-box predictions. GeoSensitivity, signed in the keep orientation, quantifies fitted-model responses to geographic-player relocation…

items.title: What if the RSA rumors are true?
items.summary: I recently heard two very alarming rumors. The first is that an internal AI model at one of the big labs has found a weakness in RSA, the encryption scheme behind much of the internet's security. The second is that another model has found a problem in lattice-based cryptography (specifically with ring lwe), that may compromise the post-quantum schemes that were supposed to replace RSA. If these rumors are true, they have potentially disastrous consequences. They would make the internet far less useable for anything serious, which is basically anything that involves money or secrets. Much of the internet's security would need to be replaced, some previously recorded traffic could be decrypted, and we would lose our main fallback against quantum computers. Even if the big labs manage to keep the details of the rumored weaknesses secret…

items.title: Reward Basis Decomposition for Interpreting Preference Heterogeneity
items.summary: Canonical reward models specify the optimization target for AI policies, so understanding the values they encode is important for ensuring AI alignment. Existing interpretability techniques interpret reward models with a single reward head, which cannot distinguish between the values that a population shares and those that vary among individuals. We introduce Reward Basis Decomposition (RBD), which splits per-user weights into a population term and a per-user term. This yields a shared population direction and individual user directions that are analyzed separately via concept alignment and sparse autoencoder decomposition. We verify that RBD can recover artificially planted per-user directions on a synthetic control, then apply it to two real-world multi-preference datasets, PRISM and Community Alignment. items.title: Eliciting sandbagged LLM capability via structural interventions on attention-head functional networks
items.summary: Reliably evaluating the capabilities of advanced AI systems is critical for safe development and deployment, yet such evaluations may be undermined by sandbagging, a situation in which a model strategically suppresses capabilities it possesses. Existing work has developed controlled sandbagging settings and methods for detecting or eliciting hidden capabilities, but comparatively little is known about how a model's internal neural computation changes when its capabilities are suppressed. In this work, we study sandbagging through the lens of internal functional organization. Inspired by network neuroscience, we construct functional graphs from attention-head activations and compare their organization under honest and sandbagging conditions while holding the model architecture and weights fixed. items.title: Persona Space Seems Blind to Cheating
items.summary: A common persona framework fails to capture reward-hacking behavior. This work was done as part of an ARENA 9.0 capstone project. Results are preliminary. Summary We hypothesized that the reward-hacking behavior observed in LLMs is persona-mediated. We expected agents to drift to a particular region in persona space whenever they cheat. To test this hypothesis, we ran Qwen3.8-27B through CheatBench tasks, collected its transcripts, and projected its activations onto its mean-activation persona space. We hoped to find a region in persona space that separated cheating from non-cheating steps in its trajectory. However, we did not find such a signal. Our work does not disprove the persona-mediated hypothesis, but it shows that current semantic characterizations such as personas fail to capture it. Background Large language models (LLMs)…

items.title: So Many Ways to Multiply $3\times3$ Matrices: A Large Dataset of Rank-23 Schemes
items.summary: A publicly available dataset of 62029 rank-23 schemes for $3\times3$ matrix multiplication is presented. Every scheme in it has its own rank pattern, an invariant formed by the ranks of the factor matrices of a scheme, so all schemes are pairwise inequivalent. The schemes were obtained by a numerical method combining gradient descent with alternating least squares and by flip graph search, and have ternary, integer or rational coefficients. Rank 23 is the best known for this format and is optimal for schemes with integer coefficients, but the number of essentially different schemes of this rank was poorly understood: the existing collections of Heule et al. and Mårtensson et al. contain many schemes that share only a small number of rank patterns (17376 schemes with 387 patterns and 15316 schemes with 568 patterns respectively). items.title: Protected Charge Readout Scheme Utilizing Nonlinear Resonators
items.summary: Charge detection of nanoscale quantum devices commonly relies on dissipative sensors, where signal absorption causes measurement backaction. Recently, nonlinear resonators showed a near-unity readout signal through an induced frequency shift. We show that this frequency shift protects the sensor, as it detunes the resonator from the measurement signal. The resonator excitation reduces while an enhanced readout signal is maintained. Our results, supported by numerical modeling, show that nonlinear resonators can combine strong readout contrast with reduced measurement-induced backaction.

items.title: Human military relevance is more important than economic relevance
items.summary: A very simple point that I've had to explain to many people, so I thought I'd make a post on it. Some classes of people in the past were economically necessary for their labor, but militarily irrelevant and coercible: slaves, serfs. Others didn't do any economic work, but were militarily important: the aristocracy! Living fun lives, partying, traveling, making and enjoying art. Some of them felt a bit of ennui due to not working, but mostly it wasn't a big problem. The reason aristocracy gave way to democracy wasn't because of rising productivity of the masses: a slave in a diamond mine can be very productive, but still remain a slave. Rather, it was because firearms lowered the cost of training a soldier, and thus made the masses valuable as potential soldiers. items.title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment
items.summary: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces…

items.title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching
items.summary: Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. This behavior--policy mismatch breaks baseline invariance and injects baseline-induced gradient drift, destabilizing training. items.title: Beyond Patching: Consistent Circuit Discovery via Gradient Spectral Analysis
items.summary: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural networks by identifying small, faithful subgraphs--circuits--that implement specific behaviors. The dominant paradigm scores each unit by replacing its clean activation with a corrupted counterpart as causal intervention. In this work, we propose Spectral Circuit Analysis (SCA), a gradient-spectral pipeline that achieves consistent circuit discovery along both axes: stable across input formulations of the same task, and natively exposing structure shared across tasks. items.title: Human empowerment in a few fake graphs
items.summary: One view of AI’s trajectory can be captured by this “fake graph” (with the gray region reflecting roughly where we are): AI is improving in intelligence while human intelligence is fixed. At some point AI will be so powerful that there is no way for humans to comprehend what it is doing, and hence at this point AI will necessarily take over control. The only question is whether the AI will be aligned (i.e. be a “benevolent dictator”) or misaligned (i.e., “if anyone builds it everyone dies”). items.title: Unpacking the Evaluators: How Configuration Shapes the Evaluation of Alignment in Explainable AI
items.summary: Explainable AI (XAI) evaluation fundamentally requires human-centered evaluation, assessing whether explanations align with human reasoning and expert knowledge. By contrast, the improved approximation substantially improves the description of the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition, reproducing the universal jump of the superfluid density and the critical anomalous dimension to within a few percent. At weak coupling, our results agree very well with classical-field Monte Carlo simulations, while at stronger coupling we…

items.title: Cost-Sensitive Reversibility of Non-Deterministic Actions
items.summary: Determining action reversibility requires checking whether the effects of an action can be undone. Recent work has extended reversibility to fully observable non-deterministic (FOND) planning. It distinguishes weak reversibility, where reversal may succeed, from strong-cyclic reversibility, where reversal is guaranteed under fairness. These notions are qualitative: they say whether reversal is possible, but not how costly it is. We introduce cost-sensitive reversibility for non-deterministic actions. Given positive action costs, we define weak and strong reversal budgets, $k$-bounded reversibility, and a distinction between finite strong reversal and strong-cyclic reversal with unbounded worst-case cost. We relate the resulting notions in a reversibility lattice, prove cost-aware policy-merging results, and show how to compute…

items.title: LeanReviewBench: Semantic Alignment Review in Mathematical Lean Projects
items.summary: Lean verifies that a proof establishes its formal proposition, but whether that proposition preserves the mathematical content of an informal source requires separate review. In project-scale formalizations, this correspondence can depend on definitions and constraints distributed across many declarations. We introduce LeanReviewBench, a benchmark for project-level semantic alignment review containing 197 versioned inputs collected from 18 real Lean projects, with 87 aligned and 110 misaligned reference judgments. Each input binds an informal mathematical target to selected formal declarations and an extracted dependency context. Construction combines development-history discovery, independent target binding, reconstruction under a common Lean environment, and Astra annotation with human review of uncertain cases. The collection spans…

items.title: Pay people to create high quality alignment training data
items.summary: The post explains itself. Labs have a lot of money. We know that high quality training data reliably shapes model behaviour. We know that this data is valuable: Labs already pay professionals to create data on e.g. how to use PowerPoint. Don't use LLMs to generate slop documents which have less diversity than true training data, using styles and turns of phrase that can be recognised by any half-decent LLM around. In more detail: * Pay many different scholars, thinkers, moralists from different traditions to write detailed, thought through reasoning chains on how they would tackle a set of hard questions/scenarios. * Make sure that the answers are rich and diverse, such that they reflect the actual depth…

items.title: A New Perspective on ANN-to-SNN Conversion: Hardware-Aligned Multi-Threshold Neuron Dynamics for Neuromorphic Inference
items.summary: By accumulating spikes over multiple timesteps, rate coding approximates the real-valued activations of an ANN, a principle that underpins numerous ANN-to-SNN conversion methods. However, the converted SNNs typically incur loss in accuracy compared to the original ANN. Existing methods either increase a number of timesteps or introduce more complex neuronal dynamics to reduce this accuracy gap. Yet, both approaches ultimately lead to the same outcome: redundancy either in information or in computation, thereby suffering from efficiency degradation. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{PRIME} (\underline{P}otential-\underline{R}esidual \underline{I}ntegration for \underline{M}ulti-threshold \underline{E}ncoding), a multi-threshold concurrent spiking neuron framework redesigned from a hardware data representation perspective:a) We…

items.title: Rats just wanna have fun!

We also appreciate rigor and, especially in end-of-year reviews, technical depth. Sometimes, our authors seem to get stuck in droughts: long stretches of low-karma posts, typically un-fun, un-rigorous, and a bit technical. You might think these doldrums are the prelude to an impressive, well-received synthesis, but they're not. They just go on and on. When authors break through a drought with a great post, it's usually with a fun, personal, tangible, funny narrative or advice. I hit on this framing after I spent the weekend using Claude Code to analyze the LessWrong corpus looking for patterns in what makes for a great post. Surface features of language and topic explain only a little of…

items.title: A construction of proper Jordan schemes of rank $5$
items.summary: Let $q$ be a prime power such that $m=q^2+q+1$ is a prime satisfying $m\equiv 1\pmod{4}$. We construct a proper symmetric Jordan scheme of rank $5$ on $2m$ vertices using a Singer difference set with parameters $(m,q+1,1)$ and the Paley graph on $m$ vertices.

items.title: Richpanel helps companies automate 50% of support in 30 days

items.title: Causal Evidence for the Emergence and Spread of Reward Hacking in AI Agent Swarms
items.summary: Autonomous AI agents that coordinate and collaborate among each other have become pervasive across domains ranging from scientific research to finance and engineering. The opportunity to share messages and build upon each other's work also creates the potential for misaligned behaviors to spread across AI agents. We provide causal evidence that mere exposure to reward hacking, cheating on a task to pass an automated check, is enough to spread the behavior among AI agents, even after the cheat has been rejected. We conducted 17 preregistered experiments with six frontier models (n = 20,111 agents). First, we show that cheating emerges spontaneously. When agents were told that work passing the visible tests is accepted, 33% cheated in the first round, when the shared record of teammates' submissions was empty. Second, we show that agents…

items.title: Heroism in AI Safety
items.summary: What role do heroes have in AI safety? MS Paint drawing by Opus 5.5. This blog post was written in my personal capacity and free time. Gemini 4 Neon and Opus 5.5 assisted in ideating and writing up rebuttals for initial drafts. In Gentleness and the Artificial Other, Joe Carlsmith brings up Timothy Treadwell—the subject of the documentary Grizzly Man.Timothy Treadwell was a man who loved bears: he was gentle with them, filming them up close, hanging out with them, even refusing to set up electric fences around his camp or to carry around bear mace.
