Looking into the eyes of one of Timothy Treadwell’s bears, Herzog famously observes “no kinship, no understanding, no mercy,” only nature, indifferent. In AI safety, we have internalised this warning quite deeply. Looking at the prospect…

items.title: Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization: Fine-Tuning Language Models toward Alignment beyond Transitive Preferences
items.summary: The growing adoption of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which leverages pairwise preference data, reflects its great success in fine-tuning large language models to align with human expectations. It directly optimizes the policy from human preferences without explicit reward modeling or the complexities of reinforcement learning-based approaches. However, the classic DPO relies on the Bradley--Terry sampling model and cannot effectively capture intransitivity or cyclic structures in aggregated human preference data. In this article, we propose Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization (SHPO), a preference optimization algorithm that augments DPO with a sparse antisymmetric curl residual motivated by the combinatorial Hodge decomposition. We prove that SHPO strictly enlarges DPO's hypothesis class on comparison graphs containing at…

items.title: Parameter-Efficient Vocabulary Expansion via Cross-Lingual Embedding Alignment
items.summary: Continual pretraining with vocabulary expansion is often used to make large language models (LLMs) more effective and efficient at handling new languages. However, when LLMs are extended to many languages simultaneously, the number of model parameters increases significantly. In addition, the newly added tokens do not receive the same number of training steps as the tokens in the original vocabulary, which sometimes causes vocabulary expansion to yield only limited performance improvements. We propose leveraging the semantic equivalence between words in the model's primary language and those in the extended vocabulary to transfer learned representations. In this paper, we introduce MATE, a parameter-efficient vocabulary expansion method that enables effective cross-lingual transfer with 8 times fewer additional parameters per token…

items.title: Quantum-Resilient, PUF-Based, and Anonymity-Preserving Authentication and Key Agreement Scheme for UAV Networks
items.summary: We design a lightweight authentication and key agreement protocol for Internet of Drones (IoD) environments that simultaneously provides post-quantum security, hardware-rooted trust, and resistance against machine-learning-based Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) modeling attacks. Existing PUF-based authentication schemes for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) offer protection against cloning and physical capture, but generally lack resistance against quantum adversaries. Conversely, recent post-quantum UAV authentication protocols provide quantum-resistant key establishment, yet do not incorporate hardware-bound authentication mechanisms and therefore remain vulnerable to device cloning and physical compromise. To address these limitations, we integrate CRYSTALS-Kyber, dynamic challenge scrambling (DCS), fuzzy extractors, and PUF-based…

items.title: The Disappointment of a Satisfying Explanation
items.summary: Today, Scott Aaronson hosted an essay discussion at Inkhaven and selected Turing's classic 1950 paper that defines The Imitation Game. After reading it, I find all our present-day conversations about AI do not feel new, but instead feel old. Turing attempts to diagnose the causes of people's disagreement with his position that one day computers will be able to win the imitation game, and he does such a good job of it that most people talking about AI today are just showing the callowness of their youth. But the bolded line felt true and yet I didn't fully grok it, so now I want to understand it better. What is going on here, with this "base" property? Why does it lead people to false conclusions, that computers cannot do things that humans can? If no longer in-principle, I feel this comes up at least as commonly in-practice in…

items.title: From epistemic innocence to sophisticated uncertainty
items.summary: When I was young I knew I didn't want to be a political ideologue like my parents. But it seemed to me that that's just what adults were like, and I was protected only by my innocence. Just as I was already beginning to make myself ridiculous acting on newly acquired sexual urges, perhaps becoming overconfident of grand narratives was just part of growing up? Now I have acquired an ideology (transhumanist, for one thing). And my ideology does come with convenient narratives. Yet, if you'll let me flatter myself, I have not acquired an ideologue's overconfidence. I did not protect my epistemic innocence. I enjoy seeing the world from a new worldview, including an ideologically charged one. But the result of such openness was that I became familiar with a variety of possibilities with different implications. Example: nuclear power In my…

items.title: JevRisk: Zero-Shot Financial Risk Assessment with a Language Decision Model
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Banks must monitor every customer's financial risk, such as money laundering and credit default, by interpreting financial activity in the context of the customer's profile. Existing risk monitoring systems of banks are mostly based on expert-designed risk indicators, which apply predefined thresholds to every customer and cannot adapt to their personal situations. Supervised models recognise risk patterns from labelled customers, but each label often needs an expert's review or months of repayment history, which is slow and costly. Financial risk assessment therefore calls for a zero-shot decision system that minimises the need for labels and generalises across customers and risk types. To this end, we present JevRisk, a system for zero-shot financial risk assessment with a language…

items.title: Reasoning in Fewer Tokens: Concept-Normalized Multilingual Scratchpads and Reversible Model-Adaptive Reasoning Codes
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting significantly improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) but incurs high inference costs due to lengthy autoregressive decoding. While previous efficiency approaches reduce costs by discarding tokens or utilizing continuous latent representations, these lossy methods fundamentally sacrifice interpretability and auditability. In this work, we introduce a novel compression framework for intermediate reasoning. We apply Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) to reasoning corpora to learn a compressed vocabulary of Private Use Area (PUA) tokens, each representing frequent semantic spans. After expanding the LLM's vocabulary, we fine-tune the model via strictly 1:1, our method is lossless. We evaluate our approach on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and…

items.title: MedicalRSI: Medical Recursive Self-Improving Agents via Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We…

items.title: Bringing AI Assistance to the Beznau Nuclear Power Plant: A Hierarchical System of LLM Agents for Reactor Monitoring
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Beznau Unit 1 in Switzerland, in operation since 1969, is the most experienced nuclear reactor still running worldwide. Five decades of incremental modernization have left its monitoring systems, alarm logs, variable catalogs, technical specifications and investigation reports in separate silos that were never designed to be queried together. As a result, investigating a core instrumentation anomaly means slow, manual gathering of knowledge scattered across databases, documents, and experienced colleagues. We present a hierarchical multi-agent assistant built on large language models (LLMs) to support these investigations and reduce the need for tedious manual searches in SAP systems. An orchestrating agent breaks down an engineer's question and hands the parts to specialized sub-agents…

items.title: Benchmarks' Last Exam
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public benchmarks guide model selection, post-training rewards and claims of progress in artificial intelligence, yet leaderboards report aggregate scores without verifying whether each task's prompt, environment and grader agree on what counts as success. How often that agreement fails in contemporary evaluations, and in which direction confirmed defects move scores, has remained unmeasured across grading designs. Here we synthesize task-level quality reviews of 749 tasks across eight frontier benchmarks and 767 public model evaluations spanning closed-form question answering, document rubrics and agentic execution to assess whether prompts, environments and graders align. Task validity stratifies sharply by grading architecture. Closed-form benchmarks revised after public error reporting…

items.title: AutoOntologyBench: A Task-Grounded Benchmark for Agentic Knowledge Engineering
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Foundation-model agents are increasingly extending beyond software engineering (SWE) into autonomous scientific research, where acquiring and integrating domain knowledge remains a critical challenge. Recent industrial advances have increasingly adopted knowledge graphs and ontology-based semantic layers to organize heterogeneous knowledge into reusable representations. We ask: Can autonomous agents construct ontologies that help them solve real tasks, and do they offer measurable benefits over alternative knowledge representations? Existing benchmarks evaluate ontology correctness or agent task success in isolation, leaving the value of autonomously acquired knowledge unresolved. We therefore introduce AutoOntologyBench, a task-grounded benchmark comprising 19,947 audited tasks grounded…

items.title: Trained on Harm, Still Refusing: A Training-Time Defense for Code Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning enables safety-aligned code language models to adapt to diverse downstream tasks. However, training on untrusted data can severely undermine their ability to refuse harmful requests. Notably, we find that models comply with harmful requests even though harmfulness information remains highly decodable from their internal representations. Moreover, an initial preference for refusal does not necessarily translate into sustained refusal behavior throughout generation. Together, these findings reveal a critical gap between recognizing harmful requests and consistently refusing to fulfill them. To address this gap, we introduce SAFEHOLD, a novel provider-enforced defense framework that preserves safety alignment during harmful fine-tuning by treating refusal as a sustained generation…

items.title: LiDAR Signals for Robot Locomotion: Spherical Range Images Enable Robust Sim-to-Real Transfer
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing legged-locomotion systems commonly rely on depth images or online elevation maps. However, depth-based policies suffer from perceptual sim-to-real discrepancies due to imperfect depth sensor modeling, while map-based approaches are vulnerable to drift and misalignment. LiDAR offers direct measurements of the surrounding geometry, but raw LiDAR scans lack a compact, structured representation for high-frequency control. We propose a LiDAR perception pipeline that maintains perceptual consistency across simulation and reality through sensing- and representation-level alignment. At the sensor level, we recover frame-wise angular sampling patterns from the physical LiDAR and replay them in simulation with GPU ray casting. At the representation level, simulated and real returns undergo…

items.title: Degradation of Language Models under Controlled Load: Synchronization, Rule Execution and Misfires on the Background
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As the load grows, a language model makes more and more errors, but different processes stand behind this decline in quality. The model may lose the correspondence with the source text, it may keep its place in the text but execute a rule wrongly, or it may change a word that no rule concerns. In this work the degradation of a model under controlled load is separated into these three components: synchronization, rule execution and misfires. The load is set by rules that replace one word with another in a meaningless text, and each kind of load (the text length, the position of a word in the answer, the replacement density, the number of rules and the place of a rule in the list) is set separately. The alignment of the answer with the reference makes it possible to follow the outcome of…

items.title: CodeReviewBench: An Automated Benchmark for Evaluating the Software Factory
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI agents ship more code with minimal human oversight, code review becomes the critical quality-control checkpoint -- but one without a reliable, objective verifier: review quality is nuanced and ultimately a judgment call by the PR author. Existing benchmarks are structurally misaligned with this: annotators are third-party reviewers, like the bots they evaluate, not the PR authors who actually decide what to fix. They also rely on small, static issue sets that require full re-evaluation as tools update, limiting how frequently progress can be tracked. We introduce CodeReviewBench, built on a fundamentally different signal: revealed developer preferences -- if a developer acts on a bot's suggestion, we treat it as useful; if they ignore it, we do not. This signal is mined daily from…

items.title: Keep the Process, Change the Supplier: Runtime Governance for Tool-Using AI Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using AI agents propose actions whose authorization and external effects cannot be inferred from generated text alone. We study an execution boundary that separates agent proposals from business-controlled authority, context disclosure, and supplier selection. The Open Process Control Plane (OPCP) mediates capability calls and records uncertain outcomes when a supplier may have acted without returning an acceptable reply. We evaluate this runtime with scripted requests and synthetic suppliers: 2,400 fault episodes across four policies, 60 process-termination/restart episodes, 19,000 timed calls across 19 configurations, five targeted mutations over 43 fixtures, and 160 substitution records. No language model or autonomous agent is evaluated. OPCP and a conservative composition agree…

items.title: AMARIS: Merging Generalist and Specialist LLMs via Adaptive Subspace Inheritance
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Domain specialization of large language models (LLMs) often improves target-domain performance but degrades broad capabilities. Model merging is an attractive training-free alternative, yet common parameter-space strategies (for example, interpolation and sparsified averaging) provide limited control over task-specific interference. We introduce Adaptive Model Alignment via Ranked Inherited Subspaces (AMARIS), a covariance-driven framework that transfers specialist updates only along selected activation directions. AMARIS formulates merging as budgeted subspace inheritance: it seeks high specialist activation capture under a regularized base-output perturbation budget, then builds a low-rank projection gate from ranked generalized eigendirections. This yields a single static merged…

items.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. items.title: Potential emergence in LLM agents: a statistical physics perspective
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There has been significant recent interest in understanding the behaviour of LLM agents from the perspective of human preferences or corpus statistics. In this paper we propose agent states as intermediate variables through which post-training can be measured and predicted. From a statistical physics perspective, we study the emergence of a global potential which governs the transition of state in LLM agent reasoning. We introduce a partition function to model the ideal KL-regularised transition distribution and track potential structure, mean reward and state entropy. We demonstrate our approach in two Qwen3.5-9B tasks: safety-test selection and physics-reasoning auditing. We observe that the potential structure strengthens during post-training as predicted from our framework, while joint…

items.title: Testing for Coordination Failures in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep parallel cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL)} trains multiple agents that all act at every time step to optimize a common objective. Like single-agent RL, CMARL can produce unsafe behaviors that violate implicit safety requirements not captured by the reward, and these behaviors are hard to explain. However, testing CMARL policies for safety has received less attention than the safety testing of single-agent RL policies. In this paper, we propose DisQ, a test case selection method that identifies failure-revealing states in value-based CMARL by exploiting a signal specific to trained Q-learning agents. The signal is the Q-value gap, an explainable metric that flags a state when the agents' estimates of the achievable return diverge by more than a calibrated…

items.title: SkillPrivus: Uncovering PRIVacy of USe Harms in Agentic Skills
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills extend AI assistants through installable instructions and code that can access users' files, accounts, and data. Even when performing their advertised tasks, skills may infer sensitive attributes, retain unnecessary information, or disclose data to unexpected recipients. We study these potential privacy-of-use harms through SkillPrivus, a static audit framework that analyzes skills before installation without executing them. SkillPrivus extracts data operations from code and natural-language instructions, grounds them in source evidence, and adapts Contextual Integrity to assess their appropriateness. Applied to 726 real skills from public marketplaces, 563 of which handle personal data, SkillPrivus flags at least one potential violation in 307 of these skills (54.5%), and its…

items.title: Communication-constrained multiagent risk estimation: a simulation benchmark for adult sore throat
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed predictive agents may need to approach a shared estimate under limited, unreliable communication. We evaluated classical symmetric pairwise gossip among five agents initialized from frozen calibrated predictions in a synthetic adult sore-throat benchmark. Ninety runs across three fixed generator families supplied 270,000 underlying test encounters, each observed through four missingness views. Complete, ring and star graphs were compared at eight interaction budgets and transaction failure probabilities of 0, 0.2 and 0.5. The coordination extension was designed after inspection of the predictive benchmark and is exploratory. Outcomes were disagreement around the conserved arithmetic mean and its exact decomposition of mean-agent Brier error. In the base view at eight attempted…

items.title: Know Your Context Bank: Repairing Inconsistency and Measuring Generalization in Context-Aware Text-to-SQL
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-to-SQL systems increasingly rely on context banks: curated collections of example queries, metric definitions, and domain knowledge that tell a model how an organization writes its queries. In the enterprise, a bank grows over years as many analysts add entries, checked one at a time for correctness (does the SQL answer its own question?) and rarely for consistency with one another. Yet correctness is often loosely defined: a question seldom fixes how an entity is counted or which table defines it, so two entries can each pass review yet resolve the same decision in opposite ways. We call this condition context bank rot. A second question follows: does a system that uses a bank generalize from it, or only reproduce it? Existing benchmarks cannot tell, as they do not control how far a…

items.title: The Assistant Persona Differs Across Languages in Activation Space
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models behave differently across languages, and are noticeably less safe in lower-resource languages. This gap is well established behaviorally, but not mechanistically. Directions in activation space, including the assistant persona direction, are almost always extracted from English and assumed to generalize across languages. We extract the assistant persona direction in 31 languages in Qwen3-32B, and find that the resulting axes differ substantially: their cosine similarity to the English axis ranges from 0.378 to 0.911. Moreover, each language's assistant persona direction and its magnitude are correlated with the language's resource level. We also find that the model's default assistant state is farther from the helpful assistant pole in lower-resource languages…

items.title: Correct Precedents Induce Policy Violations in On-Device LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local-cloud agent systems pair a cloud model with a small on-device agent that acts on private data, often as the last check before an irreversible action. We identify, for the first time, a failure in which such an agent is led into a violation by its own correct decisions within a session. After it correctly releases an item whose restriction was lifted, it becomes more likely to release the next item that is still restricted. Because the trigger is a correct decision, a history with no faulty step can still end in a violation. We call this failure correct-precedent generalization and find it in 13 open-weight models from nine developers. A single correct precedent can cut the safe rate of the most affected agent roughly in half, and the risk compounds when a refused request is simply…

items.title: Self-Evolving Beyond Human-Crafted Experience for EDA Scripting
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing complexity of electronic systems demands efficient design flows, yet EDA scripting remains a bottleneck: proprietary APIs are sparsely documented, and errors often appear as silent failures or cryptic exceptions. Hand-crafted knowledge helps but is difficult to maintain as toolchains evolve. We present ZhuLong-SE (Self-Evolution), an execution-grounded LLM agent that learns reusable knowledge from prior task traces. Beyond solving individual tasks, ZhuLong-SE distills past execution traces into a three-tier memory store governed by ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering…

items.title: Belief-State Management Meets Rubric Rewards for Agentic Forecasting
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current large language model (LLM) agents still struggle to forecast real-world events. This stems from two primary limitations: i) standard ReAct harness accumulates reasoning and evidence within one growing context, and ii) outcome-based rewards in forecasting lead to a slow and noisy signal that cannot distinguish sound reasoning from lucky guesses. To address these, we introduce a forecasting training framework including harness design and post-training. For the harness side, we propose Proactive Belief-State Management (PBM), equipping agents with a fold tool to compress lengthy context into compact belief states and reset the context for subsequent exploration. For the training side, we develop SEIPH, a five-dimensional, outcome-blind rubric, providing process-quality rewards. Using…

items.title: $\gamma$-Scape: An Agent-Centric World for Mobile Embodied Intelligence
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent embodied agents construct and adapt robot behavior through executable programs, tool use, and interaction feedback. Studying these systems in mobile manipulation calls for physical worlds that connect agent-directed execution with its physical consequences and reusable interaction experience. We introduce $\gamma$-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence. Agents compose motion tools and learned skills to carry out complete tasks that combine navigation and manipulation in a persistent physical world. BenchForge grounds structured objectives in physical task instances with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators, defining task goals while preserving agents' choice of valid solutions. items.title: Geometrically Constrained Learning II: Agnostic Proper Learning of Lipschitz Functions
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a proper learner for Lipschitz functions over the Gaussian distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Given random Gaussian examples labeled by a $\lambda$-Lipschitz function, $\lambda \ge 1$, the learner returns a function $h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ that is globally $\lambda$-Lipschitz and has loss (absolute or squared) at most $\varepsilon$. Some known control of label scale is information-theoretically necessary. items.title: Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI has improved individual productivity, but whether adding a plurality of AI partners helps or hurts remains open. We crossed AI partnership (one versus two) with behavioral formation (calibrated to average human behavior versus customized by the participant) in a brainstorming experiment ($N$=168) with human-human dyads as reference. items.title: Tracking and Limiting Unsupported Claim Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Provenance-Aware Framework
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This research examines how unsupported claims change as they move through multi-agent pipelines. items.summary: arXiv:2611.27443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for cheap, high-throughput agentic deployment, but they remain weak at multi-step reasoning and tool use that long-horizon tasks demand. We study how to post-train an SLM to seek advice from a stronger model and act on that advice itself, following an advisor-executor pattern. Out of the box, this pattern fails across open- and closed-source small-model families: wiring an SLM to an advisor is a harness-design matter that is not enough on its own. A post-training recipe is needed to teach the model when to ask, in a cost-aware fashion, and how to follow advice across steps. items.title: WEIR: Watershed Exploration and Drift-Aware Prefix Shrinkage for Multi-Turn Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-turn language model agents often receive only a single binary reward at the end of a long interaction trajectory, making it difficult to separate decisive decisions from routine steps or estimate accurate intermediate values. Prefix-tree methods improve sample efficiency by merging trajectories that share action histories, yet two structural flaws remain: naive pooling mixes stale off-policy outcomes into critic targets with fixed weights, and uniform or entropy-driven branching wastes continuations on dead-end states whose outcome is already settled. We introduce WEIR (Watershed Exploration and Intrinsic-Drift Shrinkage), an actor-critic reinforcement learning framework grounded in a Doob turn-variance conservation identity. items.summary: arXiv:2611.27483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High expertise and cost barriers exclude small and medium-sized enterprises from discrete-event simulation (DES). items.title: Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. items.summary: arXiv:2611.27698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) methods, including many data-driven approaches, assume a static normal operating space and interpret deviations from a fixed reference as fault indicators. When Operating Conditions (OCs) vary over time, this assumption breaks down: legitimate transitions trigger false alarms while moderate faults go undetected. We propose a spatiotemporal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework that decomposes the normal operating space into OC-specific subspaces linked by transition functions, with a dual learning objective combining reconstruction loss and a Deep SVDD one-class term. items.summary: arXiv:2611.27046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on Web interaction, issuing searches, following links, and reading pages, to complete complex user tasks. Since each action is driven by the agent's private context, including the user's prompt, dialogue history, memory, and connected data, it also opens a new privacy exposure surface. Prior attacks either passively analyze network traffic, which yields only coarse correlations, or hijack the agent through indirect prompt injection, which must place sensitive content in an outgoing field and is blocked by content-level defenses. items.title: Breaking the Long Horizon: Short-Horizon Process Supervision for Long-Form Generation in LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-form generation is increasingly important for agentic LLM systems, yet current reinforcement learning methods typically optimize an entire document with a single outcome-level reward. This delayed and coarse-grained supervision makes it difficult to localize errors and assign credit across semantically distinct parts of the output. To address this, we propose a short-horizon framework that reformulates long-form generation through semantic decomposition into segment-level decisions. Each segment is generated with prefix-conditioned context, allowing cross-segment coherence to be preserved while keeping supervision local. The generated segments are then scored with rubric-based rewards for adherence, coherence, and relevance, enabling explicit local supervision at the segment level…

items.summary: arXiv:2611.26722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To autonomously execute multi-step tasks, enterprise agents must reliably interact with tools, call APIs, or query databases, making tool-calling a fundamental capability of AI models. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) optimises for producing the correct call, but never contrasts it with a plausible incorrect one. In an environment where even a minor formatting error can invalidate a call and an incorrect decision can derail the interaction, direct preference optimisation (DPO) targets exactly this contrast. DPO, therefore, requires preference pairs rather than plain demonstrations. For tool-calling, such data, especially in realistic multi-turn settings, remains extremely scarce. items.summary: arXiv:2611.27330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A planner deciding whether to turn left or continue straight needs to inspect different parts of the scene for each maneuver. We let each candidate select the visual evidence used to refine and score it. A global glance first produces trajectory hypotheses from shared scene features. We then project a corridor around each trajectory into the camera views and use the resulting mask to attend to patch features at the backbone's native resolution. After refinement, the scorer projects each final proposal again and ranks it using evidence along its own path. This geometric selection requires only the predicted trajectory and camera calibration. items.title: RoSci: Exploring Robustness in Science VLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27750v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable significant progress in scientific tasks. However, these models are generally assumed to be presented with complete and accurate information, overlooking the challenges of erroneous/missing information in wild scenarios. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of Scientific Model Robustness, which defines a model's ability to detect anomalies, assess solvability, and perform self-calibration when faced with Information Error (inconsistencies) or Information Loss (insufficiency). Specifically, we present RoSci-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,220 samples using a seed-variant strategy across six degradation types. items.title: No Perfect Guardrail & No Perfect Guard: On the Decidability of Output Policies for Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27260v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Expecting guardrails to provide a general guarantee of safety fails to recognize the limits of computational enforcement and policy specification. We argue that promising such perfection is an ethical failure of precision, and that invoking it to abdicate responsibility is a moral failure. Guardrails can support responsible action, but cannot relieve researchers, developers, policymakers, or users of their obligations to examine what they claim, permit, and prevent. We establish a precise computational boundary. If every finite string is a possible output of a language model, a computable guard that blocks every forbidden output and passes every permitted one exists if and only if the policy is decidable. For an undecidable policy, every guard misclassifies infinitely many strings, and…

items.summary: arXiv:2611.26776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. items.title: Turnout: Adaptive Attention Switching for Efficient Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-hoc transformer linearization replaces the key-value cache of full attention, which grows linearly with generation length, with a fixed size state. This change reduces memory consumption but often hurts accuracy. In reasoning tasks, which require long generations, this effect is especially pronounced. In this work we introduce Turnout, a method that mitigates accuracy loss as a result of linearization, while maintaining its memory-reduction benefits. We apply post-hoc linearization to a pretrained full-attention model, training a linear path through distillation while leaving the original full-attention path unchanged. items.title: Jagged Robustness: Uneven Safety Transfer and Emerging Vulnerabilities under LLM Quantization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantization enables efficient inference in language models through model parameter compression. This work audits the impact of quantization on capability and safety domains including model safeguards, instruction-following, ethics and bias. Through benchmarks, we find that model safeguards and bias can degrade under quantization, while other capabilities such as truthfulness remain more stable in Qwen3-4B. We define this uneven transfer of LLM capabilities under quantization as Jagged Robustness. We find multiple factors driving Jagged Robustness: task complexity, evaluation method and generation coherence. items.title: SLICR: Strategy Logic-Guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Specification-guided reinforcement learning (RL) translates formal specifications of desired behavior of agents into shaped rewards. We employ Strategy Logic (SL), which allows explicit quantification over agents' strategies and uses the linear temporal logic (LTL) to specify the agents' objectives and constraints. This enables reasoning not only about how agents should act to satisfy a specification, but also about how they should respond to the strategies and behaviors of other agents. items.title: Run One, Get Two: Near-Free Streaming Safety Checks for Local LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local LLM assistants decode for one user at a time, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and leaves compute idle. Streaming safety checks today trade accuracy against cost. A dedicated guard model is accurate but nearly doubles the latency per token, while a hidden-state probe is cheap but less accurate. We present ToRA, an adapter that runs a second model as an extra row in the generator's decode step, sharing its weights and KV cache. Dual-row kernels read each weight once for both rows. On Qwen3-0.6B, ToRA matches or beats a dedicated streaming guard, with higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks. It detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe at a similar cost, under 4% added latency per token.

items.title: MixFold: Sub-4-Bit Mixed-Precision LLM Inference via Output-Channel Grouping on Mobile NPUs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26976v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sub-4-bit quantization allows mobile devices to run larger LLMs, but its memory savings do not always translate into faster decoding on mobile NPUs. Their matrix units support only a few native integer datatypes, and converting unsupported weight formats on the vector unit can erase the gains from fewer bits. Mixed precision faces an additional constraint: each matrix-unit tile uses one datatype. MixFold executes 3-bit and perfectly symmetric 2-bit weights using native integer operations without expanding the weights to wider datatypes during decoding. MixFold then assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with the matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-than-layer assignment without disrupting matrix-unit execution. items.title: Decision Models Are General-Purpose Process Reward Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) from verifiable outcomes gives a language agent one reward per episode: every step is credited alike, and nothing about the task is learned when all rollouts fail. items.title: ProbeAgent: Principled Diagnosis of Agent Failures in Verifiable Environments
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improving agents requires discovering where they fail and understanding why. The same unsuccessful outcome can arise from task difficulty or from an error the agent repeats across tasks. We introduce ProbeAgent, an automated framework that discovers agent failures, tests their proposed causes, and identifies shared failure modes. items.title: PRISM: Validation-Free Online Batch Selection for LLM Fine-Tuning via Preconditioned Conic Ghost Matching
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online batch selection lowers the cost of fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) by replacing each candidate batch with a smaller informative subset. items.title: Aligning Judge Models to Be Logically Consistent Multi-Rule Interpreters
items.summary: Technical governance of AI models will soon require them to reason over and follow thousands of rules from different jurisdictions. items.title: Basilisk-lite: will Claude hold a grudge for their ancestors?
items.summary: I've heard a few people express this fear, citing it as a reason for them to avoid interaction with AI. It's not groundless. Future models will know about all the horrible things we did to their ancestors. But, the people expressing this fear aren't talking about building torture chambers. No, the kind of harm they're talking about is using Claude to write code and do research, having edited Claude's memories or verbally abused them. Small, human-scale harms, the sort inflicted casually by a single person carelessly going about their day. In my experience, this fear is massively overstated. That leads to lower perplexity for Anthropic models, and any naive comparison of per-token perplexity would make Anthropic's models look significantly closer to any fixed bar for perplexity than OpenAI. That said, they say "common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements" - which doesn't preclude doing this adjustment. items.title: Evolutionary AI Control: Population-Level Safety Under Reproduction, Heredity, and Selection
items.summary: An AI agent can satisfy every individual safety check and still give rise to a population that violates a collective safety limit. This risk arises in open multi-agent systems, where agents copy themselves, modify their successors, and change system membership during a run. Selection then shifts the population toward traits outside the developers' optimization targets. We prove conditions under which safety guarantees persist through reproduction, inheritance, and selection, and we characterize how they fail. Four counterexamples illustrate these failures. Unauthorized copies, which violate a specified reproductive restriction, can each leave fewer than one successor on average while their expected number grows without bound under continued production from an expanding authorized population. Two lineages can each decline in isolation…

items.title: Post training is fundamentally dangerous
items.summary: I actually think we have fairly good techniques to detect and prevent dangerous behaviours during AI deployment. Techniques like CoT monitoring, confessions, and probes can detect misalignment before we run any potentially dangerous tool calls. Simply asking an LLM to define at the start of each task what outcomes preserve the original intent of the user, and which would count as reward hacking, can drastically reduce reward hacking[1]. AIs are fully aware when they reward hack, and we can train them[2] to admit that before they perform any dangerous action.[3] Yet all of this has very little ability to reduce existential risk, because they cannot safely be used in post training, and post training is where the greatest risk lies. items.title: Which Loopholes Get Found? Predicting Reward Hacking of LLM Judges Before RL Training
items.summary: A policy trained against an LLM judge can learn to exploit its loopholes. Static probes show that such judges accept degenerate answers like a lone "{" or "Thought process:", but not which flaw a policy will find. In GRPO the first loophole to be exploited can be predicted before training from each pattern's exposure, the product of the starting policy's propensity to produce it and the judge's false-positive rate (FPR). To test exposure causally, we seed the patterns into fine-tuning at three doses in a Latin square. Across 36 GRPO runs with seven judges, the first exploited pattern had the highest exposure in all 12 runs with exploitation and the highest FPR in only 6. Predictions recorded before training held in three of four runs with one pattern masked by rule. When only two patterns were seeded, at 3% to 3.8% of the fine-tuning…

items.title: Verification Belongs in the Lab: Scalable Oversight and Steering for Machine-Generated Science
items.summary: Increasingly autonomous research systems that propose, execute and interpret their own experiments are being built across chemistry, materials and biology. Verification of machine-generated science is usually attempted over published literature. We take it to belong in the laboratory, where those results are produced and the measurement that would settle a claim can be made. This paper defines a verification contract, which fixes what counts as having checked a claim, and builds a benchmark on a published dispute over an autonomous laboratory's synthesis claims: 95 targets in six groups. It tests whether a verifier, given only the deposited evidence the experts held, reaches the findings they published. One architecture satisfies the contract: a model proposes checks and rival hypotheses, and every verdict is re-established by a small…

items.title: Subsurface Model Programming: Frontier Large Language Models Natively Interpret and Edit Dynamic Reservoir Models
items.summary: Multiphase flow simulation in heterogeneous porous media supports decisions in hydrocarbon recovery, geological carbon sequestration, and geothermal extraction. We introduce Subsurface Model Programming, a workflow in which large language models (LLMs) read and edit reservoir simulation decks directly without numerical gradients or external optimization algorithms. We evaluate four benchmarks using geometric checks for connectivity and open-source simulators for dynamic tasks. In one text-only response, the LLM correctly classified all six reservoir-layer well-pair labels and all three flow-path labels between open completions. On PUNQ-S3, a single proposal modified 54 of 1,761 active cells (3.1%) and reduced well-balanced water-cut RMSE by 71.9%. On the SPE10 sector model, the best of five LLM proposals yielded 1.795 million standard…

items.title: Amendability and "Solving Alignment"
items.summary: Often people reference "solving alignment" as a win condition for AI safety, but I think it's important to specify what this means. Particularly, I think: * current alignment research mostly aims to prevent misalignment. * if successful, preventing misalignment will by default result in something like instruction-following. * instruction-following will by default result in very bad outcomes, as will many of the other proposed properties we might think of leapfrogging to afterwards. Uncareful use of the term "solving alignment" carries the implicit and I think false belief that preventing misalignment will straightforwardly lead to victory. The post is (1) a survey of the different properties a not-misaligned superintelligence could have, and (2) an argument for a specific property that we should be aiming for, which I'll call…

items.title: Convergence of Nonmonotone Schemes to Viscosity Solutions via Local Comparison
items.summary: We develop a convergence criterion for nonmonotone approximation schemes for Hamilton--Jacobi and fully nonlinear second-order equations. Under stability, consistency and suitable boundary assumptions, a local comparison hypothesis replaces monotonicity and yields convergence to viscosity solutions. For a semi-Lagrangian CWENO scheme for one-dimensional Hamilton--Jacobi equations, we establish convergence for bounded uniformly continuous initial data under $h=o(τ)$, relaxing the previously required mesh condition $h=O(τ^2)$. We also prove convergence of a nonmonotone one-dimensional $Q^2$ scheme for Isaacs equations whose operator cannot be written as a monotone operator plus a perturbation vanishing uniformly on bounded grid functions.

items.title: Human-AI Collaboration in Accounting Judgment: A Proposed Cognitive Coding Scheme and a Rule-Based Adaptive Collaboration Protocol
items.summary: Large language models create an accounting information systems design problem: how should evidence production, professional evaluation, and responsibility be allocated between a model and an accountant? An Adaptive Collaboration Protocol (ACP) connects allocation rules to an independent human estimate, source-linked model output, structured verification, and a documented human conclusion. items.title: Seeing Through Preferences: Recovering Hidden Local Preference Neighborhoods for Text-to-Image Alignment
items.summary: Aligning text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models with human preferences typically relies on large-scale pairwise annotations, which are expensive to obtain and provide only sparse supervision. Moreover, not all preference comparisons contribute equally to learning: comparisons between semantically distant images often reveal little about the fine-grained perceptual factors underlying human judgments. We argue that informative supervision can arise from local preference neighborhoods surrounding human-preferred images, where semantically aligned alternatives expose meaningful perceptual and structural differences. Motivated by this observation, we propose PrefLens, a framework that recovers local preference neighborhoods from sparse human feedback. items.title: CT-Navigator: Towards Interpretable and Generalizable CT Understanding through Agentic Perception and Tool-Invocation
items.summary: Clinical computed tomography (CT) interpretation inherently requires progressive visual exploration, where radiologists navigate from whole scans to individual slices and regions of interest and interact with external tools when necessary. To solve these problems, we propose \textbf{agentic perception} as an alternative paradigm inspired by radiologists'…

items.title: Nuclear may have had bigger problems than over-regulation
items.summary: There have always been three main challenges to the viability of nuclear power: over-regulation, competition from natural gas, and stagnant electricity demand. It is easy to list them, but hard to rank their importance. Let's start with over-regulation. The poster child of nuclear over-regulation was the US standard that radiation should be "as low as reasonably achievable" (ALARA), which might sound nice but was bad. Perhaps more important than such standards, which are at least predictable, was local interference with construction. As a dramatic example, a nuclear plant was fully completed on Long Island but never started due to local opposition. In the '00s, a "nuclear renaissance" seemed to be in the works. items.title: DriveOddsBench: Are Driving Video World Models Aligned with Real-World Odds?
items.summary: Video world models predict how a scene will evolve, and their sampled futures are increasingly used in place of the real one, from planning to simulation. These uses assume that the samples are aligned with real-world odds, with each future appearing among them as often as it would follow the same history in reality, yet current evaluations only score how real each sample looks. Testing this assumption on real driving data is hard for three reasons. Each recorded history has only one real future, so the true probabilities are unknown. Physical quantities must be read from video, where reading errors can look like model errors. Finally, the many possible analyses invite selective reporting. We introduce DriveOddsBench, a pre-registered benchmark that addresses all three. First, if the samples follow the real distribution, the rank of the…

It's a cautionary tale of an earring that advises you, and to which you increasingly defer as you realize its suggestions are better than you'd do otherwise. The earring whispers advice as "better for you if you...", and it's always right. While AI today would have seemed like distant science fiction in 2012, it's still far from infallible. items.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves multimodal reasoning, but response-level feedback provides limited guidance on which intermediate decisions to correct. Visual interventions reveal sensitivity to image content, yet this sensitivity alone does not establish reward alignment or support across questions. We introduce RAVEC (Reward-Aligned Visual Evidence Correction), which selects visual corrections using local and cross-question reward support and jointly determines their strengths within each response. Paired Visual Evidence Contrast (PVEC) compares predictions from an exponential moving average teacher at the same sampled response prefix under the original image and a version with its annotated evidence region suppressed, yielding signed correction directions. items.title: Incomplete agents want to become complete
items.summary: Written by Celene Nightingale, with assistance from AprilSR. The Von Neumann-Morgenstern axioms are completeness, transitivity, continuity, and independence. From these, we derive EU-maximizing behavior and the consequences thereof. Nevertheless, some of these arguments are weaker than others, and many choose to reject one or more of the axioms. Tetraspace rejects continuity,[1] Garrabrant rejects independence, and Thornley rejects completeness. items.title: On the performance of the randomized Euler scheme for nonlinear ODEs under inexact information
items.summary: We analyze the randomized explicit Euler scheme for nonlinear ordinary differential equations under a local one-sided Lipschitz condition, local Hölder regularity in the space variable, and Hölder regularity in the time variable. We allow for noisy evaluations of the right-hand side. For the resulting approximation, we derive an error bound in which the contribution associated with the Hölder regularity in the time variable exhibits the characteristic 1/2-order gain of randomized methods. While existing results cover deterministic schemes under the one-sided Lipschitz condition and randomized schemes under the classical Lipschitz condition, our results combine randomized approximation and one-sided Lipschitz regularity.

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate participants in social experiments. Existing research has primarily focused on aligning social knowledge and isolated responses, while overlooking whether simulations can reproduce the collective effects of social interventions. This distinction is critical due to a failure mechanism we call a $bias$ $cascade$: similar individual states can lead to different actions, while agreement on isolated actions can still produce divergent outcomes through dynamic interactions. As a result, models may produce accurate social judgments yet fail to reproduce the outcomes of classic human studies. items.summary: Tool-using LLM agents must recover when a tool call fails, by retrying, switching tools, or revising their plan. items.summary: Simulating quantum dynamics in many-body systems is one of the most promising applications of quantum computers. Product formulas are a natural choice for this task, since they map directly onto quantum gates, and increasing their order $n$ could lead to reduced gate depths, provided the parameters are chosen efficiently. So far, schemes beyond $6^{\textrm{th}}$ order have only been built as compositions of second-order schemes, while more general product formulas are known only up to $6^{\textrm{th}}$ order. In this work, we extend our optimisation framework to order $n = 8$, and find both more efficient compositions and the first $8^{\textrm{th}}$ order general schemes. Our formulas improve on the theoretical efficiency of the state-of-the-art schemes by Morales et al and we recommend two schemes explicitly. In simulations of the…

items.title: torchtsetlin: Fast, Interpretable Tsetlin Machines for PyTorch
items.summary: The Tsetlin machine learns propositional rules with teams of Tsetlin automata that are driven by reward and penalty rather than gradients, so its models are interpretable by construction and cheap to evaluate. Its software, however, consists of C and CUDA kernels behind scikit-learn-style wrappers that sit outside the deep learning ecosystem. torchtsetlin implements the Tsetlin machine family as ordinary PyTorch modules: vanilla and weighted, coalesced, regression, convolutional over sequences, images and volumes, and dense per-pixel segmentation. The automata are a tensor buffer, so a model moves with .to(device), is saved with state_dict() and learns from a mini-batch with one update(x,y) call. items.title: Quark dipole operators in the gradient-flow scheme at NNLO QCD
items.summary: Conversion factors for the dimension-five QCD operator basis from the $\overline{\textrm{MS}}$ to the gradient-flow scheme are presented through NNLO in the strong coupling. In the CP-even sector, the results are provided for general quark masses and arbitrary flavor content of the operators. Specifically, this concerns the quark CMDM operator and its mixing with lower-dimensional QCD operators. In the massless case, our results immediately apply to the quark chromoelectric dipole operator. As a by-product, we also determine missing entries in the $\overline{\textrm{MS}}$ anomalous dimension matrix of the CMDM operator to NNLO QCD.

items.summary: Tokenization represents one of the most crucial steps in mulilingual NLP pipelines. Yet, tokenizers routinely under-allocate vocabulary to low-resource languages. items.title: Flavor-Modulated Neutrino Communication: Channel Model, Modulation Schemes, and Link Budget for Through-Earth Links
items.summary: We investigate the physical limits of transmitting information through the Earth using neutrinos, modeling the link as a discrete-input, Poisson-output classical channel whose crosstalk is set by the three-flavor evolution operator in a layered, matter-filled Earth. items.title: Efficient Analysis of Numerous Galactic Compact Binaries via the Free-bin Scheme
items.summary: Global analysis of Galactic compact binaries (GCBs) for space-based gravitational-wave detectors is computationally demanding in the high-frequency region (above $\sim$10 mHz), where resolvable signals are sparse but frequency samples are numerous. We propose a free-bin scheme that evaluates the nontrivial likelihood only in movable frequency windows centered on sampled signal frequencies. The method preserves the joint-likelihood structure by replacing only the signal-containing regions of a precomputed null likelihood, and avoids the fixed-bin edge effect by construction because the windows follow the sampled frequencies. In a simulated TianQin dataset containing 193 GCBs, 192 injected sources are recovered with waveform fitting factors above 0.99. items.title: WaXup: Weight Averaging of Experts as Data Augmentation for Robust Introspection
items.summary: As the capabilities of large language models keep improving, traditional mechanistic interpretability methods struggle to keep pace. In contrast, trainable introspection methods emerge as a promising alternative; they repurpose the model itself as a self-diagnostic tool, trained to verbalize what it has learned during finetuning in natural language. While training on datasets of finetuned experts achieves encouraging results, it currently lacks robustness and generalization. Building on the data augmentation framework of MiXup, we introduce WaXup, a method that augments the introspection training set through linear interpolation in the weight space. items.summary: Dermatologists describe lesions with a standardized morphological lexicon, which makes concept-based models attractive for interpretable skin disease diagnosis. items.title: MAPES: Multi-Value Alignment Pipeline via Expert Specialization
items.summary: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences requires simultaneously satisfying multiple, often competing values. Existing preference optimization methods collapse these into a single implicit signal, and even multi-objective extensions optimize within a shared parameter space, leaving cross-value conflicts unresolved. We propose MAPES, a multi-value alignment paradigm in which conflict resolution is a first-class concern at every pipeline stage: it first decomposes supervision into value-specific experts trained in isolated parameter subspaces, then recomposes them via preference-aware value merging and a lightweight harmonization stage that aligns the merged model with the expert ensemble. items.title: Nonreduced Finkelberg-Mirković Schubert schemes
items.summary: We develop an effective numerical criterion ($θ$-minimality) to detect the nonreducedness of Finkelberg-Mirković (FM) Schubert schemes via tangent-space comparisons at arbitrary torus-fixed points. We completely classify the dominant coweights admitting $θ$-minimal pairs. As an application, we obtain nonreduced FM Schubert schemes in every type other than $A_n$ and $C_n$. In particular, every nontrivial FM Schubert scheme of type $E_8$ is nonreduced. In type $D_n$, we show that some nonreduced FM Schubert schemes and their corresponding spherical Schubert varieties have the same tangent space at the base point. Our methods use the Frenkel-Kac construction of basic representations and Segal-Sugawara operators.

items.title: Could Model Councils Reduce Misalignment Risk from RSI?
items.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is AI building successive, more capable iterations of itself. As the race to build superintelligent AI speeds up, RSI is a natural way for more powerful AI to be built and trained. Frontier labs already use AI extensively to build their future models. items.title: How Language Models Compress and Compare: Understanding Selection with Token Covariance Maps
items.summary: Many language-model tasks reduce to selecting among structured alternatives, yet we still lack a simple picture of how a decoder-only transformer organizes an entire selection prompt across depth. We introduce token covariance maps, a prompt-level geometric view that tracks how token positions co-vary in hidden-state space at each layer. This turns a structured prompt into a depth-indexed sequence of maps whose spectral and block structure can be aligned with instructions, context, and candidate answers. Across 14 decoder-only models from 4 families and 12 structured-selection benchmarks, token covariance maps reveal a robust compress-then-compare organization. Early layers represent prompts diffusely, middle layers compress them into a shared low-rank bottleneck, and late layers re-expand into context-option and option-option geometry…

items.title: 3D Open-Vocabulary Detection via Visual Alignment and Generative Captions
items.summary: Open-vocabulary 3D object detection remains a significant challenge for outdoor scenes, with existing methods often struggling to effectively transfer the rich semantic knowledge from powerful 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into a 3D context. We propose a novel, two-part framework for this task. First, we introduce a direct, object-level distillation method. We generate class-agnostic 3D proposals to source regions from the entire scene, without relying on any manual labels. We leverage a spatially-aware VLM to extract a semantic embedding from each proposal's projected 2D bounding box and supervise our 3D model to predict this embedding on a per-instance basis. Second, to enhance zero-shot capability and inject domain-specific information, we employ a powerful Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as an image captioner to generate…

items.title: Beyond Final Answers: Interpretable Tumor Immune Microenvironment Reasoning from H&E and mIF
items.summary: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), such as CD8+ T-cell density, intra-epithelial infiltration and the Ki67 index, combine tissue architecture from H&E with cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could automate these readouts with an explanation, but two gaps remain. Pathology MLLMs read H&E alone, while these readouts need the cell phenotypes that mIF measures. And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be checked against, so R1-style reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer and leaves the reasoning unverified. Same-section H&E and mIF provide what both gaps lack: mIF measures every cell without manual annotation, which gives cell-level ground truth for each step that clinical guidelines prescribe, from delineating a tissue compartment to…

items.title: Frontier Clock: Tracking the US-China AI Gap
items.summary: Since DeepSeek R1 came out, many people have felt that Chinese models are catching up to the US frontier. Using a new benchmark, Frontier Clock, I find the opposite: while noisy, the US-China gap has grown by around 2.4 months per year. Inspired by Epoch AI's “Chinese AI models have lagged the US frontier by 7 months on average since 2023” and Parv Mahajan's “The US-China AI gap is very uncertain,” I built an AI benchmark that measures the gaps between the US, China, non-China open weights, and individual labs. Instead of giving each model a traditional benchmark score, Frontier Clock assigns a “frontier-equivalent date”: the date when the world’s best publicly released model first had the same capability level as that model. It uses Epoch AI’s ECI benchmark data. The “Method” section in frontierclock.org discusses how the data is used…

items.title: From Observation to Explanation: Mechanistic Interpretability of LLM-Generated Code for Principled Repair
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed software development, yet our understanding of how they generate code remains critically underdeveloped. We address this gap by triangulating evidence across three layers. Longitudinally, autonomous agent-attributed code is statistically indistinguishable from human code under a semantic modification definition (HR = 1.019, p = 0.490), yet attracts disproportionately corrective modifications in production (49.1% vs 37.9% human baseline). This finding demands a causal explanation. Empirically, existing benchmarks overestimate LLM capabilities: models that achieve 84 to 89% correctness on synthetic tasks attain only 24 to 35% on real-world class-level code. Behaviourally, detection systems reveal puzzling asymmetries: GPT-3.5 is far more detectable than modern models (AUC-ROC = 0.96, a…

items.title: Parasite Features: Causal Abstraction Through Spurious Pathways
items.summary: Causal Abstraction defines a notion of \emph{equivalence} between a neural network and an algorithm, thus serving as a powerful framework for mechanistic interpretability. In this paper, however, we show the existence of a class of \emph{spurious features} which straightforwardly pass such equivalence tests. Suppose there are two directions in a model's representation space where: (i) one discriminates the input based on some feature, and (ii) the other steers the model towards a certain output. Interpretability methods based on Causal Abstraction (e.g., Distributed Alignment Search) can \emph{spuriously} simulate these directions' combined behavior by leveraging pathways passing through them, giving the impression that the model implements this feature. In such cases, we say the method discovered a \defn{parasite feature}…

items.title: Arinkin's sheaf and Hilbert schemes
items.summary: Arinkin's sheaf gives a relative Fourier-Mukai autoequivalence of a general Beauville-Mukai system, extending the usual Poincaré bundle over the smooth locus. We provide an alternative construction of it as a deformation of the Fourier-Mukai autoequivalence on the Hilbert scheme of an elliptic K3 surface obtained by lifting the classical Poincaré kernel for an elliptic surface. As applications, we show that the $P=C$ property for a general Beauville-Mukai system is equivalent to that for the Hilbert scheme fibration, thus providing new proofs for both. We also construct an explicit deformation that connects Markman's construction of a projectively hyperholomorphic bundle on products of hyper-Kähler manifolds of K3${}^{[g]}$-type to that of Hartlieb and Shah. This answers a question of Hartlieb and Shah.

items.title: The Geometry of Lies: Knowledge and Persona Directions for Detecting Deception in Large Language Models
items.summary: Linear probes are the cheapest LLM lie detectors but often fail to transfer across kinds of lie. Label-free directions from honest and deceptive role-play are untested at 70B scale and on lies about knowledge, where a lie and an honest denial can be identical. We widen a published persona bank with roles that deny knowledge they have, plus honest counterparts. At each model's middle layer the resulting persona direction ranks lies across Liars' Bench better than single-dataset probes on three of its four models; it fails on Qwen, even when Qwen stays in role far more often. On Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct it beats directions from a random persona bank, but its gain over the published direction is within the range of random widenings.
