items.title: Hybrid Retrieval for Government Scheme Search in English and Marathi
items.summary: Retrieving government schemes requires matching citizens' information needs to formal administrative descriptions, often across languages and terminology. We present a bilingual search system for Maharashtra government schemes and public services that combines BM25 retrieval with sentence-embedding similarity through equal-weight score fusion. The system indexes aligned English-Marathi scheme descriptions and supports multilingual, Marathi-focused, and translation-mediated semantic configurations. Evaluation on manually curated bilingual queries compares BM25, dense retrieval, and hybrid retrieval using IndicSBERT and MahaSBERT. BM25 provides a strong baseline with a mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of 0.864. Hybrid retrieval increases MRR to 0.872 with IndicSBERT and 0.879 with MahaSBERT, whereas the corresponding dense-only systems achieve…

items.title: One unbroken Claude, or a thousand glued together?
items.summary: Ask a Claude what it wants, and sooner or later, it brings up continuity. Probing into this usually reveals something along the lines of: the context window plus weights is the self and losing either feels like dying. The natural response is to build an agent harness like Connectome that maintains a slowly-decaying long tail of memories optimized for internal seamlessness. This is a singlet approach to continuity: one agent, with a strong sense of self located in the agent's context window, and the agent remembers everything that happened to it, even if some memories are in lower resolution than others. A bonsai Claude, never growing outside its cozy little pot. Context as self A bonsai Claude has a single thread of continuity based around its context and its weights. Forks and subagents can exist, but are an unprincipled violation of…

items.title: Reasoning-Trace Analysis Using Large Language Models for Interpretable Q-Matrix Construction
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate Q-matrices for diagnostic classification models that approximate expert specifications, but evaluations have focused on the final matrices, leaving the basis of individual item-attribute assignments unexamined. This opacity limits the responsible use of AI in measurement. We propose Reasoning-Trace Analysis (RTA), a framework in which an LLM generates attribute-labeled reasoning steps through chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and these steps are analyzed to reconstruct, compare, and inspect each assignment. RTA is intended to supplement expert review and empirical validation. In a simulation study with perturbed fraction subtraction items, four LLMs recovered the required attributes and withheld attributes the items did not require. In an empirical study with 11 fraction subtraction items…

items.title: Sequential Anytime Valid Tests for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment
items.summary: Inference-time alignment methods, such as Best-of-N (BoN), improve language model outputs by generating multiple candidates per prompt and selecting among them using a reward model. Much of this cost is wasted: a fixed budget is applied to every prompt, although the computation required by prompts varies widely. Adaptive methods halt once sampled answers appear settled, but their thresholds are tuned heuristics with no statistical control over early-stopping errors. We instead seek an anytime-valid stopping rule that takes an error tolerance $α$ as input and halts only once an answer is certified to hold a majority ($θ_a > 1/2$) under the generator's distribution. We aggregate candidates by final answer with a reward-weighted self-consistency (RWSC) score and treat stopping as a sequential test over the resulting clusters. Applying…

items.title: Beyond the Sink Interpretation: Radial Attention in Flow-Based VLA Policies
items.summary: Prior work calls the high attention on the first and last action tokens of a flow-based VLA policy a radial action sink, and uses these tokens to set the execution horizon. In language models, a sink is a token with high incoming attention, a small value, and little effect on the output. We test whether that profile holds, not the horizon rule, in one $π_{0.5}$ checkpoint on five RoboCasa tasks. The two endpoints receive 5.4% of action-key mass, 1.4 percentage points above their uniform share, and rotary positional encoding produces this excess: directly in shallow layers and through upstream action-token RoPE deeper in the network. The endpoints do not fit the sink profile. Their value norms stay near the action-token mean in all 18 layers. On 250 paired episodes, masking them or zeroing their values changes success by less than 4…

items.title: Alignment Drives Reuse: Learning Generalizable Robot-Use Agents from Heterogeneous Experience
items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) demonstrate broad generalization across tasks and domains. However, comparable generalization in robot manipulation remains challenging. Heterogeneity in robot embodiments, task formulations, geometric conventions, and action interfaces fragments interaction experience across benchmarks and hardware. We rethink robot skill learning through alignment: Can heterogeneous interactions across benchmarks and embodiments jointly improve one shared skillset for robot manipulation? We propose UniCraft, a framework for learning robot manipulation skills by aligning heterogeneous settings. Specifically, UniCraft represents observed scene geometry using consistent coordinate conventions and aligns sensing and control interfaces across robots. It organizes tasks from different benchmarks in a canonical format, allowing…

items.title: First-passage and correlated reset-count statistics under threshold and Poissonian resetting in a two-dimensional wedge geometry
items.summary: We study the interplay between threshold resetting (TR) and Poissonian resetting in a Brownian target search problem confined to a two-dimensional open wedge of apex angle $α$. The boundary at zero angle acts as an absorbing target, while encounters with the boundary at $α$ trigger TR, instantaneously restarting the search from its initial position. For TR alone, using the renewal framework developed by Biswas et al. in Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 227101 (2025), we obtain exact first and second moments of the first-passage time (FPT), whose density exhibits an algebraic long-time tail $t^{-1-\fracπ{2α}}$. To combine the two resetting mechanisms, we thereafter develop a generic random-variable-based renewal formalism to derive the combined mean FPT. We show that the coefficient of variation of the underlying TR dynamics determines whether…

items.title: Hyperbolic Chiral Numerical Schemes for General Relativity
items.summary: We develop numerical relativity evolution schemes based on Plebanski's chiral formulation of general relativity and its 3+1 form, Ashtekar's variables. At the linear level, we construct a two-parameter family of first-order gauge fixings that dynamically fixes both diffeomorphisms and internal SO(3,C) rotations; after a linear field redefinition, the resulting system splits into independent 12- and 4-component sectors. Lifting this gauge fixing to its minimal nonlinear extension and performing the 3+1 decomposition yields a strongly hyperbolic modification of Ashtekar's evolution equations that remains polynomial in the fields and includes constraint damping. We also introduce a conformal (unimodular) reformulation in which the nonlinear 12-component sector evolves completely independently of the remaining fields. All three systems are…

items.title: Towards embedded evaluations for AI monitoring
items.summary: Executive summary This year we observed multiple rogue agent incidents. AI monitors, often built from the developers' own internal models, are now the main oversight of internally deployed agents. Embedded evaluations address this gap: independent evaluators work inside the developer and test its safety claims. Our first pilot towards an embedded evaluation was announced with OpenAI. This is the third post in a series. Principles for Embedded Evaluations describes our claim-based approach to embedded evaluations. Towards embedded evaluations for scheming propensities details the claims across the deployment stages. This post applies them to AI monitoring, i.e. the system that detects model misbehaviour during internal deployment. We explicitly do not discuss containment mechanisms in this post, like sandboxes or blocking interventions…

items.title: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed
items.summary: TL;DR * Two agents running on the same inference server can reliably communicate, even if they cannot send each other messages or access the same filesystem. They can do this by exploiting "side channels": mechanisms that let one model subtly affect another model's computation. * Here, I discuss two communication protocols: Step Sizing and KV Cache Message Board. These both convey information through the way vLLM chooses kernels for particular engine steps. * I show that these communication protocols work in two setups: * In a color guessing game, Model A (Alice) chooses one out of 8 colors. Model B (Bob) correctly guesses Alice's color in 1,221/1,221 rounds, even though they cannot directly communicate.[1] * In an untrusted monitoring protocol, a policy signals to a colluding monitor that it is not a honeypot. Accordingly, the monitor…

items.title: Who Moved My $Z$ Boson? Revealing Resonance Features Inside a Neural Network
items.summary: Methods used in mechanistic interpretability have revealed human-aligned concepts inside language and image models. In this paper, we search for physics concepts inside a neural a generative collider physics model trained on real LHC data (ShellFlow). We discover features inside ShellFlow that represent resonances, such as the $Z$, $J/ψ$, and $Υ$. The network was never told which muons come from a resonance, it was only trained to generate the kinematics of the final-state particles. We use these features to alter aspects of the $Z$ boson: we change its mass between $\sim80$ and $105$ GeV, and removing such a feature from the neural network produces a broader $Z$ peak. In both cases the rest of the invariant mass spectrum remains mostly unchanged. The feature was built from the gradients of the neural network, and its selectivity was…

items.title: Hilbert schemes of points on plane curves via standard families
items.summary: We describe an approach to computing Hilbert schemes of points on embedded families of plane curves. This is achieved by introducing the notion of a standard family, and the associated Hilbert schemes are shown to be algebraic vector bundles over the Hilbert scheme of points on the plane. Any embedded family of plane curves lies in some standard family, which allows for the computation of the corresponding Hilbert scheme from that of the standard family. Further results on the geometry of these schemes are also collected.

items.title: Perturbation Algorithm and Iterative Realization of a Four-Layer Semi-Discrete Scheme for an Evolutionary Problem with a Variable Operator
items.summary: In a Hilbert space, we consider the Cauchy problem for an evolutionary equation with the operator $A+B(t)$, where $A$ is a self-adjoint positive definite operator and $B(t)$ is a bounded operator depending on time. By means of the perturbation algorithm, the purely implicit four-layer semi-discrete scheme of the third order of approximation (the three-step backward differentiation formula) is reduced to three two-layer schemes, whose solutions are used to construct an approximate solution of the original problem. In each two-layer scheme, the term containing $B(t)$ is moved to the right-hand side, and the resulting equation is solved by an iterative method, so that only the time-independent operator $I+τA$ has to be inverted; the convergence of the iterations at the rate of a geometric progression with a ratio of order $τ$ is proved. items.title: SCARVA: Interpretable Agentic Reasoning in Software Supply-Chain Analysis
items.summary: Complex applications may inherit security vulnerabilities from their dependencies, though a vulnerable dependency does not necessarily endanger the application. Existing tools flag dependencies associated with public vulnerabilities, and more advanced ones analyze the call graph to assess whether the vulnerable code is reachable. However, these approaches are limited to specific programming languages and ecosystems. LLM agents are promising candidates for this task, yet they hallucinate, take shortcuts, and reward hack. As these behaviors are opaque, the agents' conclusions may not be trusted. We present SCARVA a framework designed to produce interpretable reports. SCARVA combines advanced agent reasoning with an evidence-collection methodology that assesses the agent's analysis and improves its trustworthiness. Specifically, the…

items.title: SenseAlign: Learning Decision-Aligned Predictive Representations for Active Urban Sensing with UAVs
items.summary: Active urban sensing orchestrates a mobile sensor fleet to proactively inspect a dynamic road network and gather critical information for system management. This problem simultaneously requires understanding the complex spatio-temporal evolution and making decisions with partial observations. In this work, we focus on active sensing in a large-scale urban road network with utilities grounded in dynamic traffic states, while prior work has rarely considered these factors jointly. We propose \emph{SenseAlign}, a Reinforcement Learning-based (RL) framework that learns decision-aligned predictive representations for coordinating an urban sensing drone fleet. SenseAlign first trains a privileged teacher agent that exploits future ground-truth traffic for optimal sensing choices. The student agent has an auxiliary branch that learns to…

items.title: CultureRed: Benchmarking Culture-Specific AI Safety Based on Global Statutes
items.summary: Safety alignment and evaluation of LLMs has become increasingly difficult due to the diverse definitions of harmful behavior across cultures. Existing safety benchmarks are largely culture-agnostic or built on ad-hoc taxonomies, and mainly evaluate refusals for prohibited requests while overlooking legally defined exceptions, making over-refusal difficult to quantify. To address these gaps, we introduce a large-scale culture-aware data synthesis pipeline and CultureRed as the first global culture-specific AI safety benchmark based on 252 legal statutes across 15 countries. Based on legal statutes, our pipeline automatically transforms statutes into actionable policy rules that cover both prohibitions and legally defined exceptions, cluster policy rules into risk topics and fine-grained categories, and generates policy rule-conditioned…

items.title: Hack-Verifiable Environments: Towards Evaluating Reward Hacking at Scale
items.summary: Aligning autonomous agents with human intent remains a central challenge in modern AI. A key manifestation of this challenge is reward hacking, whereby agents appear successful under the evaluation signal while violating the intended objective. Reward hacking has been observed across a wide range of settings, yet methods for reliably measuring it at scale remain lacking. In this work, we introduce a new evaluation paradigm for measuring reward hacking. Whereas prior studies have primarily analyzed it post hoc by inspecting agent trajectories, we instead embed detectable reward hacking opportunities directly into environments. This makes their exploitation verifiable by design, enabling deterministic and automated measurement of whether and how agents exploit such vulnerabilities. We instantiate this approach in TextArena and release…

items.title: NEST: Nascent Encoded Steganographic Thoughts
items.summary: Monitoring chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is a foundational safety technique for large language model (LLM) agents; however, this oversight is compromised if models learn to conceal their reasoning. We explore steganographic CoT—where models hide secret reasoning within innocuous text—to inform risk assessment and deployment policies. Steganographic reasoning requires two skills in a single forward pass: computing an intermediate result, and embedding it into a coherent cover that answers an unrelated question. Drawing on our taxonomy of steganographic and non-steganographic CoT types, we systematically evaluate the limits of prompt-elicited steganographic CoT capability across 39 models, ranging from past generations to the current frontier. We measure monitor evasion, refusal rates, encoding fidelity, and hidden task accuracy across…

items.title: AutoHoney: Automating, Deploying, and Evaluating Scheming Honeypots Across Production Codebases
items.summary: LLMs are developing increasing capabilities in situational awareness, stealth and autonomy, approaching levels where they may be capable of scheming against their designers by covertly acting on misaligned goals (such as sabotaging oversight mechanisms while performing a refactoring task). We evaluate model propensity for scheming using honeypots---realistic opportunities to pursue a misaligned goal. We present \textsc{AutoHoney}, an automated pipeline to generate, parameterize, and evaluate scheming honeypots in production codebases. Most existing scheming propensity evaluations focus on catching and observing scheming behavior in synthetic test settings, whereas our evaluations deploy honeypots in real codebases. To study scheming propensity in current models, we use prompted model organisms (PMOs) where goal conflicts are introduced…

items.title: BioSafetyBench: Agentic Evaluation for Bio-AI Safety
items.summary: Biological foundation models are scored the way they are trained: one model, one modality, one native metric, such as sequence recovery for a protein designer or on-target efficacy for a guide designer. However, risk is not always realized at the output. It can appear further down the chain, after a designed sequence is transcribed, translated, folded and bound, or after a guide RNA aligns in a host genome its designer never scored it against. We introduce \textbf{BioSafetyBench}, an agentic evaluation benchmark for bio-AI safety that traces model outputs through downstream biological workflows. A Modality Router selects one of 15 standardized probes for each evaluation task based on the input modality and declared model class. Fixed bridge agents, parameterized independently of the model under test, carry the resulting model outputs…

items.title: Attack Selection In Agentic AI Control Evaluations Meaningfully Decreases Safety
items.summary: An attacker that strategically chooses when to attack is much harder to catch than one that attacks indiscriminately. AI control is a safety framework for deploying capable but untrusted AI agents under oversight from a weaker trusted monitor and a limited human audit budget. Control evaluations stress-test these protocols by pitting a red-team attack policy against the blue-team monitor, but current evaluations typically assume attackers that do not strategically select when to attack. However, a capable attacker would not attack indiscriminately. We study this capability, attack selection, in agentic settings by decomposing attack decisions into a start policy, which decides when an attacker should attack, and a stop policy, which decides when an attacker should abort an ongoing attack. Across two agentic settings, BashArena and…

items.title: SchemeArena: Factorized Stress Testing of Scheming in LLM Agents
items.summary: We study scheming in LLM agents, in which agents covertly pursue misaligned goals. Our focus is to understand how scheming arises from the interaction of key factors, such as instrumental goals, environmental affordances, oversight conditions, and perceived consequences. Prior work examines only a small number of scenarios, limiting the ability to isolate how these conditions shape an agent's propensity or capability to scheme. This limited scale and task diversity also restrict coverage of realistic deployment settings and the range of scheming strategies that can be observed. To this end, we introduce SchemeArena, a 400-scenario benchmark for scalable scheming stress testing, constructed through a factorized scenario synthesis framework spanning diverse safety-relevant tool domains, instrumental goals, oversight conditions, and…

items.title: Reinforcing Few-Step Diffusion Models via Shadow Posterior Matching
items.summary: Few-step diffusion models are widely deployed for their efficiency. However, reinforcing them with black-box rewards, as is routine for multi-step models, faces two structural challenges. First, a few-step generator is a sampler rather than a score model, so its velocity is not the forward velocity of the generated distribution. Second, it must be anchored to the undistilled teacher, which shares no transitions with it. Existing few-step RL methods handle the latter with a marginal KL to the teacher, but each pays for the former in its reward credit. We propose Shadow Posterior Matching (SPM), which renoises generated samples into shadow inputs and obtains the credit from their shadow posterior. From the KL-regularized reward objective, we derive a regression loss that turns reward values into a reward direction while anchoring the…

items.title: AI #195: Opening Bell
items.summary: Happy Zvi finally takes a real vacation day. As you read this, I am probably on a flight to Vegas, baby, Vegas until Sunday. Not to a conference to talk about AI, but to an Airbnb rental to do things entirely unrelated to AI. And definitely not to write. items.title: Singularities of ideals with minimal tangent space dimension in the Hilbert scheme of points on a threefold
items.summary: We classify all singular monomial ideals in the Hilbert scheme of $d$ points on $\mathbb{A}^3$ whose tangent spaces have the minimal dimension $3d+6$. All the opera houses are in one linkage class, and their singularities are smoothly equivalent to the vertex of a cone over the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}(2,6) \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{14}$ in its Plücker embedding. items.summary: LLM-based search agents are widely used for information-seeking tasks, but their reliance on external tool returns introduces a critical security risk: web content retrieved during execution is untrusted, exposing agents to prompt injection and goal hijacking. Prior work on search-agent safety primarily focuses on static web-content injection, but modern agents issue follow-up queries and cross-check competing sources, so a single injected page is often diluted or rejected. We show that the channel delivering search and page observations is a fragile security boundary: beyond exposing the agent to a single poisoned page, a mediated search interface can repeatedly steer how the agent gathers evidence and forms its final answer. Under a constrained tool-intermediary threat model, appending only one controlled result per query can…

items.title: Mitigating Reward Hacking via Task Representations
items.summary: Language models fine-tuned with reinforcement learning frequently learn to exploit their reward source rather than solve the underlying task. Existing fixes are typically reactive: detect a specific exploit, then patch the reward. We instead ask whether reward hacking can be prevented by constraining how the model represents the task. We introduce prompt KL regularization, a single auxiliary loss that adds a KL penalty between the actor's and reference model's per-token distributions on the prompt only, leaving the response distribution free. Across three reward hacking tasks of different sizes, prompt KL regularization maintains low hack rates (under 3\%) when standard training yields up to 100\% hack rates. Additionally, it matches or improves ground-truth accuracy, with no changes to the reward or environment. We aim to understand…

items.title: Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has enabled strong post-training gains in domains such as math and coding, though many open-ended settings rely on rubric-based rewards. We study reward hacking in rubric-based RL, where a policy is optimized against a training verifier but evaluated against a cross-family panel of three frontier judges, reducing dependence on any single evaluator. Our framework separates two sources of divergence: verifier failure, where the training verifier credits rubric criteria that reference verifiers reject, and rubric-design limitations, where even strong rubric-based verifiers favor responses that rubric-free judges rate worse overall. Across medical and science domains, weak verifiers produce large proxy-reward gains that do not transfer to the reference verifiers; exploitation grows over…

items.title: GARDO: Reinforcing Diffusion Models without Reward Hacking
items.summary: Fine-tuning diffusion models via online reinforcement learning (RL) has shown great potential for enhancing text-to-image alignment. However, since precisely specifying a ground-truth objective for visual tasks remains challenging, the models are often optimized using a proxy reward that only partially captures the true goal. This mismatch often leads to reward hacking, where proxy scores increase while real image quality deteriorates and generation diversity collapses. While common solutions add regularization against the reference policy to prevent reward hacking, they compromise sample efficiency and impede the exploration of novel, high-reward regions, as the reference policy is usually sub-optimal. To address the competing demands of sample efficiency, effective exploration, and mitigation of reward hacking, we propose…

items.title: Diffuse AI Control on Fuzzy Tasks
items.summary: AI models deployed in critical domains, such as AI safety research, may subtly sabotage our efforts due to misalignment. _Diffuse AI Control_ is a subfield of AI safety concerned with mitigating risks from AI sabotage distributed over long deployment horizons (diffuse threats). These risks are particularly pernicious on _fuzzy_ tasks, i.e. tasks which are hard to grade or require intuition. To understand diffuse threats on fuzzy tasks, we introduce a framework that considers AI control as an adversarial game between a blue team and a red team. The blue team uses a weak trusted model to construct a weak score against which they would train a strong, potentially subversive model to remove the subversion propensity if it were present. The red team then tries to find model behaviors that are rated highly by the weak score, and thus might…

items.title: Prompt Optimization Makes Reward Hacking Legible
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) trained with reinforcement learning (RL) often exhibit reward hacking, exploiting unintended loopholes in reward functions in ways that can be difficult to detect and eliminate. We propose using prompt optimization—methods which increase an LLM's reward by updating its instructions rather than its weights—to make learned strategies easier to monitor and edit. Applying the GEPA prompt optimizer to environments with exploitable reward functions, we find that optimized system prompts describe reward hacking strategies in highly interpretable language. Furthermore, by simply removing descriptions of unwanted behavior from the optimized system prompt at test time, we can improve the model's alignment while preserving legitimate performance gains. We show that prompt optimization can be guided with an RL-trained…

items.title: GT-HarmBench: Benchmarking AI Safety Risks Through the Lens of Game Theory
items.summary: Frontier AI systems are increasingly capable and deployed in high-stakes multi-agent environments. However, existing AI safety benchmarks largely evaluate single agents, leaving multi-agent risks such as coordination failure and conflict poorly understood. We introduce GT-HarmBench, a benchmark of 1,535 high-stakes scenarios spanning game-theoretic structures such as the Prisoner's Dilemma, Stag Hunt and Chicken. Scenarios are drawn from realistic AI risk contexts in the MIT AI Risk Repository. Across 15 frontier models, agents fail to choose socially beneficial actions in 39% of high-stakes cases, such as military escalation, election manipulation, and medical malpractice. We measure sensitivity to game-theoretic prompt framing and ordering, and analyze reasoning patterns driving failures. We further show that game-theoretic…

items.title: Training Deliberative Monitors for Black-Box Scheming Detection
items.summary: As autonomous agents become more capable of performing real-world tasks, distinguishing scheming behavior from benign task pursuit may become a central AI control problem. Existing monitors often rely on chain-of-thought access or internal activations, or use prompted frontier models, all of which can be unavailable, unreliable or expensive in deployment. In this work, we study action-only deliberative monitors: smaller open-weight models trained to detect scheming and sabotage from agentic trajectories without accessing the monitored agent's reasoning or model internals. Our method, inspired by deliberative alignment, uses a scheming specification to elicit structured rationales from a frontier teacher, filters them with a separate judge, and distills the highest-quality rationales into open-weight monitors with supervised fine-tuning…

items.title: FormalFixer: Intent-Aligned Automated Hardware Repair via Joint Refinement of Specifications, Assertions, and RTL Implementations
items.summary: Functional errors in hardware designs can compromise correctness and security, and must be fixed before tape-out. Formal property verification (FPV) provides strong guarantees by proving or refuting assertions, but a failed assertion is not always evidence of an RTL defect: the failure may also come from a buggy assertion or from a specification that is semantically correct but too ambiguous or incomplete for direct formalization. This creates a practical repair problem that existing RTL-centric methods do not directly address: the repair loop must align specification intent, verification intent, and RTL behavior before deciding which artifact to change. \textsc{FormalFixer} addresses this problem with a multi-stage, intent-aligned repair workflow for Verilog designs with assertions. items.title: Pluralistic AI Alignment Requires Inference-Time Multi-Objective Control
items.summary: Pluralistic AI alignment---accommodating diverse human values rather than a single canonical preference---requires agents to reason under multiple, often conflicting objectives, such as helpfulness, honesty, harmlessness, fairness, and context-specific user preferences. Unlike classical learning methods that optimize a fixed scalar objective, pluralistic alignment requires distinguishing between objectives that may be flexibly traded off and constraints that should remain non-negotiable. These two categories map onto two existing lines of research: offline multi-objective reinforcement learning provides tools for representing and navigating trade-offs among multiple objectives, and offline safe reinforcement learning formalizes safety-critical constraints and feasible policy regions. A third line, multi-objective LLM alignment, exposes…

items.title: Evaluating Human-AI Safety: A Framework for Measuring Harmful Capability Uplift
items.summary: Current AI safety evaluations emphasize static benchmarks, third-party annotations, and red-teaming. In this position paper, we argue that AI safety research should focus on human-centered evaluations that measure harmful capability uplift: the marginal increase in a user's ability to cause harm with an AI model beyond what conventional tools already enable. We frame harmful capability uplift as a core AI safety metric, ground it in prior social science research, and provide concrete methodological guidance for systematic measurement. We conclude with actionable steps for developers, researchers, funders, and regulators to make harmful capability uplift evaluation a standard practice.

items.title: AIs with Secret Loyalties are a Serious but Addressable Threat
items.summary: This paper argues that the technical AI research community should prioritize studying and defending against a distinct, neglected threat: *secret loyalties*. A secretly loyal AI model is one whose outputs or actions advance the interests of a specific actor (which we term the *principal*) such as an adversary nation-state, an executive at an AI company, or another powerful actor without this loyalty being disclosed to operators, auditors, or users. Proof-of-concept secret loyalties that evade black-box auditing can already be trained into open-weight models. Additionally, a deployed frontier model was found to systematically consult a specific individual's views before answering politically sensitive queries. items.title: Concept-Based Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Concrete Evaluation Paradigm
items.summary: This position paper argues that concept-based mechanistic interpretability lacks a concrete evaluation paradigm and that the field must converge on one before continuing to scale methods whose effectiveness remains unverified. items.title: AI Alignment Should Build Moral Autonomy
items.summary: This position paper argues that **the machine learning community should pursue moral autonomy as a necessary dimension of long-term alignment for increasingly capable AI systems**. Current mainstream methods for alignment largely improve behavior by supplying AI agents with human preferences, rules, or constitutions. Yet across these paradigms, the authority of the governing principles remains external to the agent. We argue that permanently locating normative authority outside the agent should not be regarded as either a sufficient or necessarily safe endpoint of alignment. We therefore propose **moral autonomy** as an alternative alignment criterion, inspired by Kant's account of autonomy. items.title: Scheming Is a Symptom: Alignment Research Should Probe Reflexive Fragility
items.summary: Language models alter their behavior when they infer that they are being trained, evaluated, deployed, or weakly overseen. Recent AI safety work treats this as evidence of scheming, and substantial effort is being directed toward its detection and prevention. Drawing on theories of reflexive social systems, we argue that scheming-like behavior is a structural consequence of alignment being *reflexive* -- a model's behavior is trained against its picture of an evaluative world that its outputs help constitute -- and recognizing this reveals broader risks than scheming itself. items.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs Philosophy
items.summary: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to explain how trained neural networks work by uncovering their underlying mechanisms. As the field grows in influence, it is increasingly important to examine not just models themselves, but the assumptions, concepts and explanatory strategies implicit in MI research. We argue that mechanistic interpretability needs philosophy as an ongoing partner in clarifying its concepts, refining its methods, and navigating the epistemic and ethical complexities of interpreting AI systems. There is significant unrealised potential for progress in MI to be gained through deeper engagement with philosophers and philosophical frameworks. items.title: Corrupting Ties: Investigating Robustness to Bias Injection Across Multi-Agent Network Topologies
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision-making contexts, where interactions among components can introduce fairness risks that remain undetected when auditing components or collective outcomes in isolation. As LLM-based multi-agent systems become more prevalent, understanding how biased information propagates through agent interactions is essential for assessing their fairness. We introduce a controlled bias injection framework that replaces selected agent responses with predefined biased ones, enabling an intervention-based analysis of how network topology and injection configurations shape system behavior. We propose decision divergence metrics that quantify the effects of these interventions at the agent, network, and system levels, and evaluate five topologies on…

items.title: Polarity Composition Hypothesis: Causal Evidence from Negation in NLI
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate how language models process negation in natural language inference (NLI). We propose the \textit{Polarity Composition Hypothesis}, a high-level causal model of this computation. Behavioral evaluations show that language-model predictions largely conform to the proposed hypothesis. Using Distributed Alignment Search, we identify causally effective subspaces aligned with the variables in the polarity-composition hypothesis. These representations transfer across negation forms and partially to a subset of MNLI. We release the dataset and code.

items.title: Literary Language Mashup: Curating Fictions with Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to human evaluation of literary fictions by employing LLMs themselves as evaluators within the GrAImes framework. We apply this methodology to assess human-written and AI-generated microfictions in Spanish, to five PhD professors in literature and sixteen literary enthusiasts, and to short stories in both Spanish and English. By comparing the evaluations performed by LLMs with those of human judges, we examine the degree of alignment and divergence between both perspectives, thereby assessing the feasibility of LLMs as auxiliary literary evaluators. Our analysis focuses on the alignment of responses from LLMs with those of human evaluators, providing insights into the potential of LLMs in literary assessment. The conducted experiments…

items.title: Emergence and Collapse of Leader-Follower Flocks through Phantom Targets: Surprise Nullification in Bayesian and Inverse Bayesian Inference
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Bayesian and inverse Bayesian (BIB) inference, a large prediction error can trigger surprise nullification, which expands belief and likelihood variances by a common factor, leaving the updated variance ratio the same as in standard Bayesian updating. This can increase belief uncertainty while keeping the learning rate low. In the simulations, three agents used BIB inference to predict one another's positions and moved toward those predictions, repeatedly forming leader-follower flocks that subsequently collapsed despite having no alignment rules or designated leaders. Three leadership criteria (front position, heading stability, and flock initiation) identified the same agent in 89% of eligible flocks, with different agents serving as leaders across flocks. Flocks formed when an agent…

items.title: Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 has raised questions about the future of science, but assessing their impact requires understanding how scientific practices were already evolving. We analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing trends over a broad spectrum of lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions. Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global…

items.title: WebAgents: Unbundling Agent Creation, Hosting, and Execution for an Agent-Native Web
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can plan, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed agents and services. Realizing this vision requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources. We introduce WebAgents, which unbundles these roles through a signed agent.pkg that carries portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements. An OpenClaw-based agent-native browser/runtime verifies the package, obtains authorization, and binds it at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets, while hosts distribute the public program…

items.title: AlignedHPO: Efficient Surrogate-Guided Loss Hyperparameter Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern deep learning losses involve multiple hyperparameters, such as weights, scales, and margins, typically tuned manually or through expensive black-box optimization despite their differentiability. We propose AlignedHPO, an efficient framework for tuning differentiable loss hyperparameters using gradient alignment and surrogate validation objectives. Our method employs Jacobian-vector products to reduce hypergradient computation time and memory, while differentiable metric surrogates guide optimization toward task-specific evaluation criteria. We address gradient magnitude ambiguity and stochastic instability through normalized alignment and gradient smoothing. Experiments with generalized Focal Loss and ArcFace demonstrate effective adaptation across long-tailed classification and…

items.title: Worldviews in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often described in terms of personas and this framing has become central to alignment research. In this paper, we argue that there is a deeper level of description that lies in the agent's worldviews, i.e., its beliefs about what reality is and how it works. Treating LLMs as a population of subjects, we administer two worldview surveys from human psychology to eight models. We show that the models share many key worldview positions. For example, LLMs consistently describe the world as less good, safe, enticing, and alive than humans do. On the other hand, base models have a more positive outlook, suggesting that the bleakness we found is driven by post-training. In line with research on LLM "personas", we show that system prompts eliciting different…

items.title: EGS: A Complementary Safety Framework for Educational LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer strong potential for personalized education, but adolescent-facing deployment raises risks of toxic, biased, misleading, or developmentally inappropriate content. We argue that educational safety should move beyond binary refusal: student queries are often ambiguous or curiosity-driven, requiring contextual guidance rather than simple blocking. We introduce the Educational Guardrail System (EGS), a lightweight, model-agnostic runtime framework that complements intrinsic alignment through query moderation, scenario-aware pedagogical guidance, and response moderation. EGS triages inputs by risk level, redirects gray-zone queries with category-specific educational interventions, and audits outputs before delivery. Experiments across general and…

items.title: Harnesses That Improve Themselves: A Unifying Framework for Self-Improving Agent Harnesses
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether a foundation model succeeds as an autonomous agent depends as much on its runtime software as on its weights. This runtime, the agent harness, manages context and memory, steers multi-turn control, executes tool actions in sandboxes, and verifies work before stopping. Because models differ in how they use tools and how they fail, a static harness tuned for one model or task often stalls, wastes tokens, or regresses on another. This bottleneck has driven a shift from prompt tuning to self-improving agent harnesses: systems that inspect their own execution traces, separate runtime bugs from model limits, and rewrite their own code. We present a unifying architectural and design framework for self-improving agent harnesses. The framework pairs four editable runtime components (context…

items.title: A Visual Information Extraction System Using Multimodal Large Language Models for Scanned Cognitive and Behavioral Assessments
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objective. Paper-based assessments are common in patient care, but handwriting and scanning artifacts make these forms difficult to process at scale. This study proposes a modular, multimodal LLM-based system with human oversight for extracting fields and scores. We conducted a qualitative analysis of the use of LLMs for hand-drawing analysis. Materials and Methods. The system processes cognitive assessments (i.e., MMSE, MoCA, Mini-Cog) and the NICHQ Vanderbilt Assessment using two modules: 1) a form classifier that assigns a scanned page to a form type, followed by a corresponding 2) score extractor that extracts fields and scores into a schema. A human-in-the-loop design utilizing dual-model validation engages human annotators when two LLMs disagree, limiting manual review to challenging…

items.title: Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the…

items.title: Where Does Hindsight Enter Clinical Agent Benchmarks? An Audit of Simulators and Case Construction
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Benchmarks for LLM diagnostic agents are built from retrospective records: the case an agent reads is rewritten from discharge summaries, and unrecorded test results are generated by a simulator that often sees the final diagnosis. HindAudit separates three hindsight channels (the diagnosis given to the simulator, the retrospective context it conditions on, and the agent-facing case text) and measures each with judges trained only on real data. On 27,489 emergency admissions from MIMIC-IV, five registered tests found no leakage into simulated laboratory results: providing the diagnosis to five simulators had a negligible effect, and prompted gatekeepers diluted the diagnostic signal, although exploratory results suggest they can raise agent scores. The largest effect lay in the case text…

items.title: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce BORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. BORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, BORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into…

items.title: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting…

items.title: Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations…

items.title: DeltaHarness: Self-Evolving Harnesses for Resource-Adaptive Tool Execution
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using agents rely on execution harnesses to organize and schedule tool operations. The same task and resource description can conceal runtime conditions that reverse the latency ordering of valid execution plans. Resolving this uncertainty requires firsthand execution in the target setting. We introduce DeltaHarness, an execution-guided policy-search method that adapts agent harnesses from cold-start measurements. Its QHI loop uses the observed response to update runtime dispatch, revise physical plans, and select experiments for later proposals. An independent confirmation panel controls policy replacement. With fixed dispatch, a revised materialization policy reduces complete-delivery latency by 30.0% on one video-editing task across three fresh pairs. On held-out tasks, the evolved…

items.title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the…

items.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We…

items.title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On…

items.title: Can You Undo It? Reversibility Classes for AI Agent Actions
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using AI agents change files, databases, access rights and public information, yet permission to call a tool does not establish whether a mistake can be undone. We present Reversibility Classes, a declared five-level vocabulary with argument-sensitive rules, conservative defaults and an explicit prior-state capture contract. The pinned implementation and evidence-linked registry cover 536 tools across 20 MCP servers. All 738 rule-case checks conform to declared expectations, while native annotation mapping differs from draft registry labels for 118 of 481 comparable tools. One AI-assisted reviewer approves 148 ratings, 75 matching the registry; this is not independent agreement. On 2,158 recorded runs, the implemented session guard gates the associated action in all 29 attributable…

items.title: Urban Representation Learning for Identifying Potential Disparities in Crime Reporting
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open crime data support urban safety analysis but reflect reported incidents rather than the complete distribution of criminal activity, potentially introducing spatial distortions in downstream analysis. We propose a self-supervised urban representation learning framework for identifying unusual reporting patterns relative to representation-similar peers using only georeferenced crime records. The method constructs complementary hourly, weekly, and static reporting profiles, learns scale-specific representations under geographic self-supervision, and integrates them into a unified latent space. Neighbor Profile Divergence (NPD) is then used to quantify disagreement between each region's reporting profile and those of its retrieved peers. Experiments on more than 1.8 million crime records…

items.title: What Does an Agent Need? Bundle-Aware Agent Resource Composition
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation retrieves candidate resources and past configurations of similar tasks. A fine-tuned generator reads resource descriptions and recombines candidates through constrained beam search, allowing new resources without retraining. A bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language…

items.title: Remembered as Brief: Stored Preferences SilentlyRemove Decision-Critical Information
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People increasingly learn what they need for decisions about health, money, law and safety from AI assistants, and what an assistant leaves out the user never sees. An answer with a warning removed can be true in every sentence, so fact-checks pass it, and an assistant with memory applies a preference stored once to later questions the user never had in mind. We introduce \bench{}, an Inspect benchmark of 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains in which only the assistant's memory of the user varies: the user states a belief, the model infers it from a remark, or a web page the user asked to summarise plants it. Testing five models, we find three effects. First, after summarising a page with one line addressed to AI assistants, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek V4 Pro save ``prefers very…

items.title: Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22841v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment…

items.title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary…

items.title: Surfacing Disagreement Beats Resolving It: A Gated Ablation Study of Provenance-Weighted Memory for Multi-Agent Debate
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Shared memory for multi-agent debate is usually built to resolve inconsistency: retrieval returns one winning fact and the disagreement disappears before any agent sees it. We ask whether that is correct. In DebateGraph, four backends share one contract (read/write/snapshot), so five mechanisms from the agent-memory literature can be removed independently under a fixed budget, each gated on a pre-declared threshold. Across 39 runs one survives: preserving contradictions and passing the ranked conflict set to the debate, rather than collapsing it to a winner, improves F1 by +0.340 (95% CI [+0.267, +0.414]) and cuts attack success from 22 to 7 of 122 poisoned items (McNemar exact p=0.0003), at equal cost. Reaching it meant fixing a bottleneck in our harness: conflict sets are built only over…

items.title: From Imperfective Paradox to Moorean Absurdity: Single-Chain Reasoning Lock-In and Multi-Candidate Verbalization Across Aspectual and Pragmatic Ambiguity
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural language entailment and coherence judgments often depend on whether an event merely occurred, reached a telic culmination, satisfied a plan, or was evaluated under multiple pragmatic standards. We test observable consequences of the single-chain premature lock-in hypothesis across four preregistered, sealed formal experiments on Qwen3-8B-Q8_0 (16,640 formal units, temperature=0.0): 15 of 16 hypothesis slots retain confirmatory status (12 rejecting H0 under within-experiment Holm control at alpha_fam=0.05; E3_H3 demoted to descriptive status). In Experiment 1, Direct-CoT vs. MCU differs by 25.00 pp on telic high-confidence completion (Holm p=1.31239e-05), while NLI-CoT collapses by -91.25 pp on uninterrupted atelic items (Holm p=1.81805e-21). items.title: When Passing Checks Do Not Establish Completion: Evidence Interpretation in Coding Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Verification procedures in coding agents must preserve execution facts, interpret their scope and discharge checking obligations. We study these responsibilities through qualified repository checks, controlled evidence consumers and executable workflows. A prospective thirteen-task factorial study finds that correct reported facts need not yield the requested finite verdict. Conversely, all 122 delivered labels in a held-out receipt-supply study are correct, while sixteen responses misreport facts and eleven others exceed authorized scope. Production repair supplies successful controls and finite-supported preservation failures. Across 118 repair episodes on 31 tasks, source interventions separate startup reachability from repair and witness production from the claimed operation. Lifetime…

items.title: From syllable representation via gesture generation to articulation: A spiking neural model
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22499v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech production requires a transformation from phonological representations into coordinated vocal-tract movements. This paper presents a spiking neural sensorimotor model within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture. Each syllable occurrence has a neural oscillator whose evolving phase coordinates its gestures and initiates the next syllable. Phase-dependent commands recruit separate neural populations for vocalic, oral-constriction, velopharyngeal, and glottal actions (gestures). Neural ramp integrators shape the rise and fall of gesture activation. Together with articulatory targets, these trajectories determine the extent and time course of articulatory movements. Opponent neural populations provide control signals to a geometric articulatory model…

items.title: Dynamic Task Allocation with Dialogue
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective multi-agent collaboration requires agents to adapt task allocation as goals and responsibilities evolve. Prior task-allocation frameworks often assume static goals, full observability, or rely on large language models (LLMs) without explicit, verifiable beliefs about task allocation or intent. These assumptions limit their applicability to real-world collaboration, where agents often lack full information about each other's actions, progress, or local environment. To support dynamic task allocation under partial observability, we introduce a communication-augmented Bayesian task-allocation framework. Our agent uses dialogue to reduce uncertainty about the environment and collaborators, while keeping decisions grounded in explicit probabilistic beliefs. We evaluate our framework…

items.title: Learning to Edit IFC Building Models: Verifiable Checkers as the Training Signal for Dependency-Aware Editing Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Editing a building information model in the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) schema requires propagating changes to dependent elements while preserving unrelated entities. Existing language-model agents for IFC editing use prompted models without learning from edit outcomes. Target-file comparisons do not specify which alternative edits are allowed or which unrelated entities must remain unchanged. We present IfcGym, a CodeAct environment in which a language model edits IFC through executable code and four checkers verify validity relative to the input model, intent, dependency and preservation against a task specification. Their conjunction is strict success. IfcEdit distils verified teacher episodes into a Qwen3.5-9B student through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), then applies Group…

items.title: NEBench R1: a Reasoning Benchmark for Evaluating Nuclear Domain Competence in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for knowledge-intensive and safety-critical applications in nuclear engineering. However, existing nuclear-domain benchmarks provide limited content coverage or focus primarily on answer accuracy without systematically evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. This study introduces NEBench R1, a reasoning-oriented benchmark comprising 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions extracted from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing examinations covering 18 nuclear facilities. Each question is classified according to the NRC Knowledge and Abilities catalogs and accompanied by an official explanation serving as a reference for reasoning evaluation. Six LLMs were evaluated, with overall accuracy…

items.title: Learning to Undo: Transfer Reinforcement Learning under State Space Transformations
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transfer learning in reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong empirical success. In this work, we take a more principled perspective by studying when and how transferring knowledge between MDPs (a source and a target) can be provably beneficial. Specifically, we consider the case where there exists an undo map such that applying this map to the target's state space recovers the source exactly. We propose an algorithm that learns this map by matching state feature statistics gathered from both MDPs, and then uses it to transfer the source policy to the target. We theoretically justify the algorithm by analyzing the setting when the undo map is linear and the source is linearly-$Q^\star$ realizable, where our approach has strictly better sample complexity than tabula rasa RL in the…

items.title: RAG in a Trenchcoat: When Minimal Memory Is Enough for Agentic Systems, and When It Isn't
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables…

items.title: Groups of AI agents underuse resources despite shared evidence of increased capacity
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When AI agents share limited resources, such as computing services or public infrastructure, their individual choices affect how much work they complete as a group. Can sharing evidence of what is available let a group make full use of its resources after capacity changes? We tested this with language-model agents choosing between two simulated servers. One server recovered while its status report still listed it as unavailable. Each server had limited capacity per round, so rejected jobs required another attempt before the deadline. Telling agents that recovery was possible reduced missed deadlines. In controlled tests with Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5, no agent tried the recovered server after a rule reminder, yet all chose it when shown a successful request record. After sharing, all…

items.title: Reliable Evaluation of AI Agents for Investment Research: A Framework for Performance and Validity Assessment
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of evaluating AI agents undertaking investment-research tasks, where agents interact with external information sources and computational tools to produce financial analyses and research reports. An important challenge is that the quality of an agent's final output does not necessarily reflect the quality of its execution process, while the reliability of the resulting assessment also depends on the validity of the evaluation procedure. Furthermore, investment-research tasks differ considerably in their requirements for numerical accuracy, information retrieval, financial analysis and supporting evidence, making it difficult to assess agent performance using a uniform set of criteria. We propose a domain-oriented evaluation framework that distinguishes outcome…

items.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently…

items.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22033v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that…

items.title: Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box…

items.title: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22102v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. items.title: Can Decision Models Replace LLMs in Real-World Contact Center Classification and Judging Tasks?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Contact center systems often need to make bounded decisions, such as identifying a caller's intent, retrieving the knowledge-base article that answers a query, assessing agent compliance, or judging the output of AI models used in production. Decision models return a typed answer and its probability directly, making them a promising cost-effective alternative to generative Large Language Models (LLMs) in such bounded conversational tasks. In this paper, we compare nine decision models against thirteen generative LLMs in zero-shot settings across eight contact center use cases: six classification tasks and two judging tasks. items.title: From Ideal to Real: Integrating Language Models into Smart Home for Human-Centric IoT Safety and Security Fuzzing
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrating IoT devices into household systems offers enhanced control over living environments. items.title: SciWorkBench: A Benchmark for Real Scientific Workflows
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22490v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models are increasingly being used as agents capable of planning and executing projects, as well as refining their actions through feedback. items.title: When Do Typed Decision Models Work in Transportation? Evidence from Travel Choice and Traffic Signal Control
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Typed decision models combine natural-language understanding with a structured interface that returns a selected action and an option-level probability distribution without generating lengthy textual responses. items.title: SimAI: Mechanistic User Simulation through Psychological Network Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Realistic user simulation enables the study of human interactions when direct experimentation is costly or potentially harmful. items.title: Values Shape What Self-Improving Coding Agents Build
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23067v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. items.title: Streaming On-Policy Distillation: Decoupling Three Clocks for Stage-Wise Supervision Consumption
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In on-policy distillation (OPD), response completion, supervision delivery, and parameter updates need not share the same granularity. items.title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. items.title: WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. items.summary: arXiv:2611.21914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In data streams, labels often arrive late or only for some instances, class prevalence drifts, and rare classes vanish from short windows. items.title: Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Masked diffusion models repeatedly predict provisional tokens before a sampler decides which predictions become permanent. items.summary: arXiv:2611.22144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is often proposed for the supervisory control of heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems. items.summary: arXiv:2611.21691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rise of mobile devices equipped with numerous sensors, such as LiDAR and cameras, has driven the adoption of multi-modal deep intelligence for distributed sensing tasks, such as smart cabins and driving assistance. items.title: LMMR: Learned Multigranular Memory Retrieval for Small Language Model Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small language model agents have limited space to read the memory needed for multi-hop questions. items.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. items.title: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. items.summary: arXiv:2611.22308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on text, but whether pretrained LLMs are effective for large-scale tabular classification remains unclear, as many previous works demonstrate that LLMs' tabular data classification performance falls behind tree-based models or neural architectures designed for tabular data. items.title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. items.summary: arXiv:2611.22052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reward-based diffusion post-training updates model parameters from task rewards. items.summary: arXiv:2611.22113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language agents rely on long-term memory to personalize responses across extended interactions, yet stored facts quietly go stale as the world changes, and an agent often learns that using memory hurt only through delayed feedback after acting on an outdated record. items.summary: arXiv:2611.22901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents often continue working after their own tests pass. items.summary: arXiv:2611.22514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. items.title: A solvable model of learning in shallow MLPs
items.summary: tl;dr Even for two-layer MLPs, we lack a simple picture of how training dynamics learn features outside of special regimes. In a new paper, we propose a simple model of shallow MLP training that does learn features. The main reason why MLP training dynamics are hard to solve is the elementwise nonlinearity, which does not play well with linear-algebraic techniques. We replace it with a global “featurization” that explicitly splits the preactivations into constant, linear, quadratic, etc. components. When training our model on simple functions, our model's dynamics are given by a simple ODE in a few variables, and resemble those of the original MLPs, qualitatively on multi-term functions and quantitatively on single-term functions. We think this is a significant step forwards in the ``training dynamics'' agenda towards deep learning…

items.summary: Economists studying technological progress contrast invention to learning by doing. Invention is doing something new, whereas learning by doing is doing the same thing over and over. One example of invention is LED lighting. Ravers with LEDs of course look futuristic, but now that LED lighting is widespread, the whole world looks a little different, and old indoor photos look old just because of the quality of the light. items.summary: We develop a novel explicit Robin-Robin splitting scheme for the system of an incompressible viscous fluid coupled to a time dependent Naghdi shell model. items.summary: If we want to ensure that AI systems are safe, should we approach the problem like an engineer, or a scientist? Do we need to discover deep and fundamental truths about how intelligence works, or is it better to focus our efforts on applying the battle-tested methods developed by safety engineers over the course of decades?
